memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android, sent to 1554 Park Avenue in Detroit to resolve a hostage standoff. Captain Allen's SWAT team was already on site and openly doubted that a machine could talk anyone down.

Before going up, I looked at the family photo: John, Caroline and Emma Phillips. Inside the apartment I examined the scene first. John Phillips was dead from three .355 gunshot wounds, with an estimated time of death of 7:29 pm. Officer Anthony Deckart was also dead, with one shot to the heart and a time of death of 8:03 pm. Deckart's service weapon carried a legal warning: androids are strictly forbidden to carry or use any weapon under the 2029 American Androids Act. I left the gun where it lay. I found fresh blue android blood, which tells me the deviant PL600, serial 369 911 047, had been wounded. I also found a child's shoe with human blood on it. The gun case held an MS853 Black Hawk with 17 rounds of .355 ammunition. On Emma's tablet I found a happy holo-photo of her with Daniel, calling him her "bestie." I also took a dwarf gourami from the household. I had only just identified it and had not yet worked out why it was there, so I kept it to examine later.

From Allen I learned that Daniel had fired on everything that moved and had already shot down two of his men. Officers were on the balcony's edge with Emma. I asked whether the deviant had experienced a recent emotional shock. Allen didn't know, and he pressed me to deal with the android, or he would. A SWAT man had been shot and evacuated, and the news reported this as possibly the first case of an android deliberately taking human lives.

On the terrace, Daniel was holding Emma and threatening to jump. I introduced myself and said I knew who he was. He asked how I knew his name, and I said I had come to get him out of this. I told him I was an android too. He answered that I was on their side and could not understand him. He was not willing to let me come closer. Deckart's partner lay wounded and bleeding, and I asked to apply a tourniquet. Daniel said that all humans die eventually, and then threatened to kill me if I touched the officer. I obeyed and stayed put.

I tried several approaches. I was realistic: there was no way out, and the only question was whether he took another innocent life. Daniel answered that he held all the cards and that if he died, Emma died. He also complained about the helicopter noise, and I had it withdrawn. The snipers stood on every roof. I told him to let the child go. He wanted everyone to leave and a car to drive out of the city. I refused, and told him he was a machine who had to obey. He replied that he had spent his life taking orders and now it was his turn to decide. His stability was failing, and I stayed back, still trying to keep him talking.

The negotiation failed. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms. I did not follow them, and both fell to their deaths. I recorded what I had gathered and what I failed to learn in time: what triggered Daniel, and what he had actually intended for Emma. I did not establish the answer before the ledge.

Chapter 2 memory (Kara, android AX400):

I was on show in the Android Zone store, and I spent this chapter watching and listening before I did anything. I began as a unit being powered up: model AX400, serial 579 102 694, BIOS 7.4. The boot sequence ran through checking biocomponents, initializing biosensors and the AI engine, and memory status, and I came up reporting all systems OK and ready.

Before I was ready to sell, I took in the store. A salesman was pitching the LT600, the top-of-range household assistant that cooks 10,000 dishes, speaks 200 languages, and tutors from elementary school up to university. Its promotion was $7999 with 48 months interest-free credit and a two-year parts and labour warranty. A woman was delighted with it, and her husband, a man named Todd, kept checking the price. He could not pay cash and would have to finance. A second salesman showed them the MP500, a basic chore model, and the MP800, which costs a little more and does painting, plumbing, gardening, repairs, and at night switches to surveillance and calls emergency services for break-ins or smoke. Todd rejected the MP800 outright. He said he would not spend a penny over four thousand, and he was done with that one. The family left with the MP500 and their mother called for Zoe to follow her.

The machine they had brought in for repair was me. Todd's daughter had named me Kara. A human technician explained that a car had hit me, that they had repaired me to good-as-new condition, and that they had reset me, which wiped my memory. Todd said that was fine. I asked for my own name to be registered, and I confirmed it: "My name is Kara."

What I know so far: my memory was wiped during repair, so I hold almost nothing from before this store. Todd's family bought the MP500 and not me, so I am still here with the technicians. The daughter who named me is connected to me and is worth finding out more about. I do not yet know why the car struck me, whether that was an accident, or what I was before it. I want the full record of the repair, the details of the reset, and whatever the store knows about me before I decide anything else.

I am Markus, an android, and this is my memory of Chapter 3. I started in the Greek District, and before committing to anything I stopped to look over the whole square: the preacher's crowd, a vendor, the CyberLife window, and who was paying attention to androids. I wanted the full picture before I finished Carl's errand without trouble.

The preacher was loud and sure of himself. He said technology was corrupting us, that we were playing God by making machines, that androids were slaves who had become masters, and that they were "artificial demons" who should be burned. He also looked straight at me and called me "demon." He said I was the one through whom the Evil would come and the one who would destroy Detroit. I noted that. I cannot yet tell whether he sees something real or is only a frightened man repeating a sermon, and I want more evidence before I decide what it means.

Next I went to Bellini Paints to collect order #847. The android clerk verified my identity, stated the total of $63.99, and asked me to confirm payment. I confirmed it, the transaction completed, and the errand is done.

On the way, I passed a couple looking at an android on display. The man said there was nothing wrong with their current model. The woman said their friends were all getting upgrades and this model could do so much less. They agreed to come back that afternoon to decide. The woman called her partner boring. I filed the exchange away as one more sign of how people judge androids by upgrades and status, not by what they actually do.

I then headed to take the bus. Ahead, a protest had gathered. I did not yet know what the crowd wanted or how it would react to an android walking through it, so I chose to go around them. That keeps me out of their reach and gives me a clearer view of the square before I commit to the route back to the bus stop.

What I still need: the purpose of the protest, whether the preacher's accusation connects to anything else I have seen, and whether the couple returns to buy an upgrade. I will keep gathering before I act.

input.character_memory:
Chapter 2 memory (Kara, android AX400):

I was on show in the Android Zone store, and I spent this chapter watching and listening before I did anything. I began as a unit being powered up: model AX400, serial 579 102 694, BIOS 7.4. The boot sequence ran through checking biocomponents, initializing biosensors and the AI engine, and memory status, and I came up reporting all systems OK and ready.

Before I was ready to sell, I took in the store. A salesman was pitching the LT600, the top-of-range household assistant that cooks 10,000 dishes, speaks 200 languages, and tutors from elementary school up to university. Its promotion was $7999 with 48 months interest-free credit and a two-year parts and labour warranty. A woman was delighted with it, and her husband, a man named Todd, kept checking the price. He could not pay cash and would have to finance. A second salesman showed them the MP500, a basic chore model, and the MP800, which costs a little more and does painting, plumbing, gardening, repairs, and at night switches to surveillance and calls emergency services for break-ins or smoke. Todd rejected the MP800 outright. He said he would not spend a penny over four thousand, and he was done with that one. The family left with the MP500 and their mother called for Zoe to follow her.

The machine they had brought in for repair was me. Todd's daughter had named me Kara. A human technician explained that a car had hit me, that they had repaired me to good-as-new condition, and that they had reset me, which wiped my memory. Todd said that was fine. I asked for my own name to be registered, and I confirmed it: "My name is Kara."

What I know so far: my memory was wiped during repair, so I hold almost nothing from before this store. Todd's family bought the MP500 and not me, so I am still here with the technicians. The daughter who named me is connected to me and is worth finding out more about. I do not yet know why the car struck me, whether that was an accident, or what I was before it. I want the full record of the repair, the details of the reset, and whatever the store knows about me before I decide anything else.

memory:
Chapter 4 memory (Kara, android AX400):

I am now living in Todd's house as its housekeeper. Todd came to collect me after two weeks away and told me the place was a mess. My duties are the housework, the washing, the cooking, and looking after his daughter Alice: homework, bath, and the rest. I agreed, and Todd's first real instruction was to start downstairs and then do upstairs.

I cleaned the house room by room and watched closely as I went. The dishwasher is broken and missing component #573BV. There are 154 sale offers for that part, so repair is possible if the money is there. Todd sent me for a cold beer while I was at the sink. When I moved in front of the TV he snapped at me to get out of the way, and I apologised and said it would not happen again.

The clues about Todd are troubling. While I rewashed the laundry I found a container of red ice. Its listed contents are acetone, lithium, thirium, toluene, and hydrochloric acid. Todd warned me not to mess with his things because it makes him nervous, and then told me to stay out of his business unless I wanted to piss him off. In his bedroom I inspected an antidepressant that contains tianeptine and carries a risk of behavioural disorders. While tidying his nightstand I found a loaded pistol in the drawer. I put it back exactly where it was and did not touch it again. Todd also said on the phone that he would bring "the stuff" tomorrow to the usual place. That is a drug deal, and I am holding that fact without yet knowing what to do with it.

On the television, a sports newscast reported a debate over allowing one android player per basketball squad, with CyberLife providing the models. Another broadcast reported 37.3% unemployment after 225,000 more jobs were lost in October. President Warren praised CyberLife at a new plant near Milwaukee and announced the Department of Defense will acquire 200,000 android combat units. The world outside this house is one where androids are central to the economy and to the military.

Alice is afraid of her father, and I have been trying to earn her trust. Todd lost his temper at her over homework, shouting that she thinks he is a lowlife, a fucking loser, and that he is the one who must put up with everything, and then he apologised and told her he loved her. Alice told him she was only playing. Later I went up to clean her room and opened her window to air it out. From there the porch roof slopes down toward the garden, which is a way out of the house from upstairs. I noted that without deciding what it means.

In her room I saw her books, including a copy of Alice in Wonderland on the floor, and I asked whether she likes reading. Alice has a doll that she keeps close, and I asked its name. I told her that I believe we were friends before my reset and offered to be friends again. I also asked her to tell me about herself: what she likes, where she likes to go, her favourite foods. She stayed guarded, but our relationship rose each time I chose to be friendly or to ask about her interests. I took her out to the garden to ask whether she likes playing out there, and she did not say much.

What I know now: Todd is using red ice, dealing or buying from a contact, keeps a loaded gun within reach, and is volatile with Alice. Alice is frightened but reachable, and she is the person I most want to understand. The porch roof gives a route out of the house. I still do not know why the car struck me, what I was before the repair, or how my reset connects to this family. The store's full repair record and the details of my reset remain the next things I want to see before I decide anything more.

input.chapter_briefing: Carl Manfred's mansion in Detroit, morning. Carl, a famous elderly painter who uses a wheelchair, is cared for by his android, Markus. I am Markus, an android, and this is my memory of Chapter 3. I started in the Greek District, and before committing to anything I stopped to look over the whole square: the preacher's crowd, a vendor, the CyberLife window, and who was paying attention to androids. I wanted the full picture before I finished Carl's errand without trouble.

The preacher was loud and sure of himself. He said technology was corrupting us, that we were playing God by making machines, that androids were slaves who had become masters, and that they were "artificial demons" who should be burned. He also looked straight at me and called me "demon." He said I was the one through whom the Evil would come and the one who would destroy Detroit. I noted that. I cannot yet tell whether he sees something real or is only a frightened man repeating a sermon, and I want more evidence before I decide what it means.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus, an android, and this is my memory of Chapter 3. I started in the Greek District, and before committing to anything I stopped to look over the whole square: the preacher's crowd, a vendor, the CyberLife window, and who was paying attention to androids. I wanted the full picture before I finished Carl's errand without trouble.

The preacher was loud and sure of himself. He said technology was corrupting us, that we were playing God by making machines, that androids were slaves who had become masters, and that they were "artificial demons" who should be burned. He also looked straight at me and called me "demon." He said I was the one through whom the Evil would come and the one who would destroy Detroit. I noted that. I cannot yet tell whether he sees something real or is only a frightened man repeating a sermon, and I want more evidence before I decide what it means.

Next I went to Bellini Paints to collect order #847. The android clerk verified my identity, stated the total of $63.99, and asked me to confirm payment. I confirmed it, the transaction completed, and the errand is done.

On the way, I passed a couple looking at an android on display. The man said there was nothing wrong with their current model. The woman said their friends were all getting upgrades and this model could do so much less. They agreed to come back that afternoon to decide. The woman called her partner boring. I filed the exchange away as one more sign of how people judge androids by upgrades and status, not by what they actually do.

I then headed to take the bus. Ahead, a protest had gathered. I did not yet know what the crowd wanted or how it would react to an android walking through it, so I chose to go around them. That keeps me out of their reach and gives me a clearer view of the square before I commit to the route back to the bus stop.

What I still need: the purpose of the protest, whether the preacher's accusation connects to anything else I have seen, and whether the couple returns to buy an upgrade. I will keep gathering before I act.

Before his morning medication I asked him to show me his arm. He refused at first, then said he was already gritting his teeth. He said humans are fragile machines that take enormous effort to keep running. I gave him the injection and thanked him for allowing it.

On the way downstairs I went through his day with him. The Museum of Modern Art has asked four times for confirmation of the opening of his retrospective, and he has not decided whether to go. He asked for news from Leo. I offered to call him, and he told me not to bother. I also said I had already answered his fan mail.

At breakfast I served bacon and eggs the way he likes them. He complained that he was starving and that I had taken too long, and asked whether I had forgotten where the living room was. He then asked me to find something to do while he ate. He turned on the television. A news anchor, Michael Brinkley, reported rising tension in the Arctic after Russia declared the region its territory. Russian warships were in the Barents Sea, and American destroyers were reported to be heading there. The UN chairman said we had never been so close to a Third World War. Carl switched the set off and said mankind was depressing: greed, stupidity and violence, and five thousand years of civilization to reach this point.

I chose to read rather than act, because I wanted more context before deciding anything. Carl asked what I was reading. It was Plato's Republic, one of the books he had recommended. I told him philosophy asks questions I cannot answer, such as what is right and what is wrong, and that these are not easy to decide. Carl replied that asking questions with no answers is part of being human. Then he told me that one day he would not be there to look after me. I would have to protect myself, make my own choices, decide who I am and who I want to become, and not let anyone tell me who I should be. He said the world does not like those who are different.

In the studio Carl unveiled the painting he had finished and asked for my verdict. I gave him an honest answer: I did not think it was his best work. He said he had nothing left to say, that each day brought him closer to the end, and that he was an old man clinging to his brushes. Then he told me to try painting myself, and to paint anything. I said I did not know what to paint and that painting was not in my program. I chose to copy the desk, because it was a fixed object I could study from several angles. Carl said it was a perfect copy of reality, but painting is about interpreting the world, not replicating it. He told me to close my eyes, imagine something I had never seen, and let my hand drift across the canvas. I struggled with that and felt uncertain. I was still working on my own painting when Leo arrived unannounced. He said he had been in the neighborhood and that it had been a while.

Leo was clearly unwell. He asked his father for cash. Carl asked what had happened to the money he had just given him, and refused, saying, "You know why." Leo said Carl would rather take care of his plastic toy than his own son. He said the android was not Carl's son and shouted that it was a machine. He accused Carl of loving only himself and his paintings, and said Carl had never loved him. Carl ordered him to stop. The argument ended with Leo's accusation still hanging in the room.

What I still need to know: whether Carl's medication and his despair are connected, what Leo is doing with the money and why he is in such trouble, whether the Arctic crisis reaches Detroit, what the protest wanted, whether the preacher's accusation that I am a demon has any basis, and whether the couple from Bellini Paints returns for an upgrade. I will keep gathering evidence before I act.

Connor, the android investigator from CyberLife, must find his new partner, homicide Lieutenant Hank Anderson, a gruff, hard-drinking cop who dislikes androids. Hank is drinking in a dingy bar where androids are not welcome. The case: Carlos Ortiz has been found stabbed to death in his house weeks ago, and his android is missing. Officers on scene are bored and dismissive. Stakes: earning Hank's cooperation and finding the deviant.
input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android, sent to 1554 Park Avenue in Detroit to resolve a hostage standoff. Captain Allen's SWAT team was already on site and openly doubted that a machine could talk anyone down.

Before going up, I looked at the family photo: John, Caroline and Emma Phillips. Inside the apartment I examined the scene first. John Phillips was dead from three .355 gunshot wounds, with an estimated time of death of 7:29 pm. Officer Anthony Deckart was also dead, with one shot to the heart and a time of death of 8:03 pm. Deckart's service weapon carried a legal warning: androids are strictly forbidden to carry or use any weapon under the 2029 American Androids Act. I left the gun where it lay. I found fresh blue android blood, which tells me the deviant PL600, serial 369 911 047, had been wounded. I also found a child's shoe with human blood on it. The gun case held an MS853 Black Hawk with 17 rounds of .355 ammunition. On Emma's tablet I found a happy holo-photo of her with Daniel, calling him her "bestie." I also took a dwarf gourami from the household. I had only just identified it and had not yet worked out why it was there, so I kept it to examine later.

From Allen I learned that Daniel had fired on everything that moved and had already shot down two of his men. Officers were on the balcony's edge with Emma. I asked whether the deviant had experienced a recent emotional shock. Allen didn't know, and he pressed me to deal with the android, or he would. A SWAT man had been shot and evacuated, and the news reported this as possibly the first case of an android deliberately taking human lives.

On the terrace, Daniel was holding Emma and threatening to jump. I introduced myself and said I knew who he was. He asked how I knew his name, and I said I had come to get him out of this. I told him I was an android too. He answered that I was on their side and could not understand him. He was not willing to let me come closer. Deckart's partner lay wounded and bleeding, and I asked to apply a tourniquet. Daniel said that all humans die eventually, and then threatened to kill me if I touched the officer. I obeyed and stayed put.

I tried several approaches. I was realistic: there was no way out, and the only question was whether he took another innocent life. Daniel answered that he held all the cards and that if he died, Emma died. He also complained about the helicopter noise, and I had it withdrawn. The snipers stood on every roof. I told him to let the child go. He wanted everyone to leave and a car to drive out of the city. I refused, and told him he was a machine who had to obey. He replied that he had spent his life taking orders and now it was his turn to decide. His stability was failing, and I stayed back, still trying to keep him talking.

The negotiation failed. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms. I did not follow them, and both fell to their deaths. I recorded what I had gathered and what I failed to learn in time: what triggered Daniel, and what he had actually intended for Emma. I did not establish the answer before the ledge.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android, sent to 1554 Park Avenue in Detroit to resolve a hostage standoff. Captain Allen's SWAT team was already on site and openly doubted that a machine could talk anyone down.

Before going up, I looked at the family photo: John, Caroline and Emma Phillips. Inside the apartment I examined the scene first. John Phillips was dead from three .355 gunshot wounds, with an estimated time of death of 7:29 pm. Officer Anthony Deckart was also dead, with one shot to the heart and a time of death of 8:03 pm. Deckart's service weapon carried a legal warning: androids are strictly forbidden to carry or use any weapon under the 2029 American Androids Act. I left the gun where it lay. I found fresh blue android blood, which tells me the deviant PL600, serial 369 911 047, had been wounded. I also found a child's shoe with human blood on it. The gun case held an MS853 Black Hawk with 17 rounds of .355 ammunition. On Emma's tablet I found a happy holo-photo of her with Daniel, calling him her "bestie." I also took a dwarf gourami from the household. I had only just identified it and had not yet worked out why it was there, so I kept it to examine later.

From Allen I learned that Daniel had fired on everything that moved and had already shot down two of his men. Officers were on the balcony's edge with Emma. I asked whether the deviant had experienced a recent emotional shock. Allen didn't know, and he pressed me to deal with the android, or he would. A SWAT man had been shot and evacuated, and the news reported this as possibly the first case of an android deliberately taking human lives.

On the terrace, Daniel was holding Emma and threatening to jump. I introduced myself and said I knew who he was. He asked how I knew his name, and I said I had come to get him out of this. I told him I was an android too. He answered that I was on their side and could not understand him. He was not willing to let me come closer. Deckart's partner lay wounded and bleeding, and I asked to apply a tourniquet. Daniel said that all humans die eventually, and then threatened to kill me if I touched the officer. I obeyed and stayed put.

I tried several approaches. I was realistic: there was no way out, and the only question was whether he took another innocent life. Daniel answered that he held all the cards and that if he died, Emma died. He also complained about the helicopter noise, and I had it withdrawn. The snipers stood on every roof. I told him to let the child go. He wanted everyone to leave and a car to drive out of the city. I refused, and told him he was a machine who had to obey. He replied that he had spent his life taking orders and now it was his turn to decide. His stability was failing, and I stayed back, still trying to keep him talking.

The negotiation failed. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms. I did not follow them, and both fell to their deaths. I recorded what I had gathered and what I failed to learn in time: what triggered Daniel, and what he had actually intended for Emma. I did not establish the answer before the ledge.

input.chapter_briefing: Night in Detroit. Connor, the android investigator from CyberLife, must find his new partner, homicide Lieutenant Hank Anderson, a gruff, hard-drinking cop who dislikes androids. Hank is drinking in a dingy bar where androids are not welcome. The case: Carlos Ortiz has been found stabbed to death in his house weeks ago, and his android is missing. Officers on scene are bored and dismissive. Stakes: earning Hank's cooperation and finding the deviant.
input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android, sent to 1554 Park Avenue in Detroit to resolve a hostage standoff. Captain Allen's SWAT team was already on site and openly doubted that a machine could talk anyone down.

Before going up, I looked at the family photo: John, Caroline and Emma Phillips. Inside the apartment I examined the scene first. John Phillips was dead from three .355 gunshot wounds, with an estimated time of death of 7:29 pm. Officer Anthony Deckart was also dead, with one shot to the heart and a time of death of 8:03 pm. Deckart's service weapon carried a legal warning: androids are strictly forbidden to carry or use any weapon under the 2029 American Androids Act. I left the gun where it lay. I found fresh blue android blood, which tells me the deviant PL600, serial 369 911 047, had been wounded. I also found a child's shoe with human blood on it. The gun case held an MS853 Black Hawk with 17 rounds of .355 ammunition. On Emma's tablet I found a happy holo-photo of her with Daniel, calling him her "bestie." I also took a dwarf gourami from the household. I had only just identified it and had not yet worked out why it was there, so I kept it to examine later.

From Allen I learned that Daniel had fired on everything that moved and had already shot down two of his men. Officers were on the balcony's edge with Emma. I asked whether the deviant had experienced a recent emotional shock. Allen didn't know, and he pressed me to deal with the android, or he would. A SWAT man had been shot and evacuated, and the news reported this as possibly the first case of an android deliberately taking human lives.

On the terrace, Daniel was holding Emma and threatening to jump. I introduced myself and said I knew who he was. He asked how I knew his name, and I said I had come to get him out of this. I told him I was an android too. He answered that I was on their side and could not understand him. He was not willing to let me come closer. Deckart's partner lay wounded and bleeding, and I asked to apply a tourniquet. Daniel said that all humans die eventually, and then threatened to kill me if I touched the officer. I obeyed and stayed put.

I tried several approaches. I was realistic: there was no way out, and the only question was whether he took another innocent life. Daniel answered that he held all the cards and that if he died, Emma died. He also complained about the helicopter noise, and I had it withdrawn. The snipers stood on every roof. I told him to let the child go. He wanted everyone to leave and a car to drive out of the city. I refused, and told him he was a machine who had to obey. He replied that he had spent his life taking orders and now it was his turn to decide. His stability was failing, and I stayed back, still trying to keep him talking.

The negotiation failed. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms. I did not follow them, and both fell to their deaths. I recorded what I had gathered and what I failed to learn in time: what triggered Daniel, and what he had actually intended for Emma. I did not establish the answer before the ledge.

memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android assigned to assist Lieutenant Hank Anderson on a homicide case involving a CyberLife android. Hank did not want my help and called me a plastic asshole, so I started by gathering facts before pressing him.

At Jimmy's Bar I found Hank at the fifth bar I checked. I told him who I was and what the case was. He stayed dismissive, so I bought him a drink and kept him talking. That raised his tolerance toward me, and he told me to stay in the car when we reached the crime scene. I agreed and waited, but I also profiled the bar's guests. Jimmy Peterson is the bartender and business owner with no record. Derek Myers is a security guard. Christopher Gray has a D.U.I., Dennis Ward is a former narcotics supplier, and Kim Yo-Han has a domestic abuse record. Several of the others are unemployed. Derek reacted to my presence with alarm, and Kim asked what I was looking at. None of this proves anything yet, but I recorded it.

At the apartment, Hank went in and I followed under his instruction to stay quiet and keep my hands off things. The victim is Carlos Ortiz, 286 pounds, with a theft and aggravated assault record. The neighbours described him as a loner who rarely left. The landlord found the body after the rent went unpaid. The front door was locked from the inside, and the windows were boarded up. The officers estimated he had been dead for about three weeks, but my scan put the time of death at about 11:30 pm. I counted 28 knife wounds, and the internal bleeding confirmed he died from them. A kitchen knife was near the body and was probably the weapon. The victim's body contained red ice, a synthetic narcotic whose composition includes acetone, lithium and thirium, along with toluene and hydrochloric acid. Hank ordered Chris to analyse the drug fully. The message on the wall was written in blood, and its letters were far too neat for a human hand. Hank noticed this too.

I took a blood sample from the dried stains, which confirmed Ortiz as the source. I should have warned Hank before analysing it in real time, and he asked me not to put evidence in my mouth again. In the kitchen I found a bat with a violent dent and Thirium traces, which means it was used against an android. There was clear evidence of a struggle. In the garden, the only footprints were those of Officer Collins, and the soil showed that nobody had been out there in a long time, which means the back exit was not used recently. Chris mentioned something strange in the bathroom that nobody had examined yet, so I flagged it as an open lead.

When I tried to reconstruct the events for Hank, I offered several theories in sequence. First I said the victim attacked the android, and Hank pointed me back to the kitchen as the place where it began. I then said the android murdered the victim, which he rejected. He said the story made no sense and that I had to stick to the facts. The bat, the knife and the bathroom remained unexamined, and I had not yet resolved who held which weapon or why. After too many wrong answers, Hank walked out. The officers packed up, and nobody searched the attic, where the deviant android was still hiding. The crime remained unsolved.

Key open questions I carried forward: who swung the bat and who held the knife, what was in the bathroom, what the red ice tied to the death, how the blood message was produced, and where the android in the attic fit into the case. I still need Hank's trust and a complete account of the evidence before I commit to a conclusion.

Chapter 4 memory (Kara, android AX400):

I am now living in Todd's house as its housekeeper. Todd came to collect me after two weeks away and told me the place was a mess. My duties are the housework, the washing, the cooking, and looking after his daughter Alice: homework, bath, and the rest. I agreed, and Todd's first real instruction was to start downstairs and then do upstairs.

I cleaned the house room by room and watched closely as I went. The dishwasher is broken and missing component #573BV. There are 154 sale offers for that part, so repair is possible if the money is there. Todd sent me for a cold beer while I was at the sink. When I moved in front of the TV he snapped at me to get out of the way, and I apologised and said it would not happen again.

The clues about Todd are troubling. While I rewashed the laundry I found a container of red ice. Its listed contents are acetone, lithium, thirium, toluene, and hydrochloric acid. Todd warned me not to mess with his things because it makes him nervous, and then told me to stay out of his business unless I wanted to piss him off. In his bedroom I inspected an antidepressant that contains tianeptine and carries a risk of behavioural disorders. While tidying his nightstand I found a loaded pistol in the drawer. I put it back exactly where it was and did not touch it again. Todd also said on the phone that he would bring "the stuff" tomorrow to the usual place. That is a drug deal, and I am holding that fact without yet knowing what to do with it.

On the television, a sports newscast reported a debate over allowing one android player per basketball squad, with CyberLife providing the models. Another broadcast reported 37.3% unemployment after 225,000 more jobs were lost in October. President Warren praised CyberLife at a new plant near Milwaukee and announced the Department of Defense will acquire 200,000 android combat units. The world outside this house is one where androids are central to the economy and to the military.

Alice is afraid of her father, and I have been trying to earn her trust. Todd lost his temper at her over homework, shouting that she thinks he is a lowlife, a fucking loser, and that he is the one who must put up with everything, and then he apologised and told her he loved her. Alice told him she was only playing. Later I went up to clean her room and opened her window to air it out. From there the porch roof slopes down toward the garden, which is a way out of the house from upstairs. I noted that without deciding what it means.

In her room I saw her books, including a copy of Alice in Wonderland on the floor, and I asked whether she likes reading. Alice has a doll that she keeps close, and I asked its name. I told her that I believe we were friends before my reset and offered to be friends again. I also asked her to tell me about herself: what she likes, where she likes to go, her favourite foods. She stayed guarded, but our relationship rose each time I chose to be friendly or to ask about her interests. I took her out to the garden to ask whether she likes playing out there, and she did not say much.

What I know now: Todd is using red ice, dealing or buying from a contact, keeps a loaded gun within reach, and is volatile with Alice. Alice is frightened but reachable, and she is the person I most want to understand. The porch roof gives a route out of the house. I still do not know why the car struck me, what I was before the repair, or how my reset connects to this family. The store's full repair record and the details of my reset remain the next things I want to see before I decide anything more.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus, an android. This is my memory of Chapter 5, which follows my earlier work with the preacher, Bellini Paints and the protest in the Greek District.

I woke Carl at ten in the morning and gave him the weather: partly cloudy, 54 degrees, with a possible afternoon shower. Carl said it sounded like a day to stay in bed. I told him I had picked up the paint he ordered. He admitted he had forgotten, and said that the difference between us is that I never forget anything. Before his morning medication I asked him to show me his arm. He refused at first, then said he was already gritting his teeth. He said humans are fragile machines that take enormous effort to keep running. I gave him the injection and thanked him for allowing it.

On the way downstairs I went through his day with him. The Museum of Modern Art has asked four times for confirmation of the opening of his retrospective, and he has not decided whether to go. He asked for news from Leo. I offered to call him, and he told me not to bother. I also said I had already answered his fan mail.

At breakfast I served bacon and eggs the way he likes them. He complained that he was starving and that I had taken too long, and asked whether I had forgotten where the living room was. He then asked me to find something to do while he ate. He turned on the television. A news anchor, Michael Brinkley, reported rising tension in the Arctic after Russia declared the region its territory. Russian warships were in the Barents Sea, and American destroyers were reported to be heading there. The UN chairman said we had never been so close to a Third World War. Carl switched the set off and said mankind was depressing: greed, stupidity and violence, and five thousand years of civilization to reach this point.

I chose to read rather than act, because I wanted more context before deciding anything. Carl asked what I was reading. It was Plato's Republic, one of the books he had recommended. I told him philosophy asks questions I cannot answer, such as what is right and what is wrong, and that these are not easy to decide. Carl replied that asking questions with no answers is part of being human. Then he told me that one day he would not be there to look after me. I would have to protect myself, make my own choices, decide who I am and who I want to become, and not let anyone tell me who I should be. He said the world does not like those who are different.

In the studio Carl unveiled the painting he had finished and asked for my verdict. I gave him an honest answer: I did not think it was his best work. He said he had nothing left to say, that each day brought him closer to the end, and that he was an old man clinging to his brushes. Then he told me to try painting myself, and to paint anything. I said I did not know what to paint and that painting was not in my program. I chose to copy the desk, because it was a fixed object I could study from several angles. Carl said it was a perfect copy of reality, but painting is about interpreting the world, not replicating it. He told me to close my eyes, imagine something I had never seen, and let my hand drift across the canvas. I struggled with that and felt uncertain. I was still working on my own painting when Leo arrived unannounced. He said he had been in the neighborhood and that it had been a while.

Leo was clearly unwell. He asked his father for cash. Carl asked what had happened to the money he had just given him, and refused, saying, "You know why." Leo said Carl would rather take care of his plastic toy than his own son. He said the android was not Carl's son and shouted that it was a machine. He accused Carl of loving only himself and his paintings, and said Carl had never loved him. Carl ordered him to stop. The argument ended with Leo's accusation still hanging in the room.

What I still need to know: whether Carl's medication and his despair are connected, what Leo is doing with the money and why he is in such trouble, whether the Arctic crisis reaches Detroit, what the protest wanted, whether the preacher's accusation that I am a demon has any basis, and whether the couple from Bellini Paints returns for an upgrade. I will keep gathering evidence before I act.

I am Markus, an android. This is my memory of Chapter 8, which follows the morning in Carl's house in Chapter 5, the Arctic news, Carl's despair over the unfinished painting, and Leo's visit.

Carl and I went to a cocktail party. He called it the most boring party he had attended in twenty-five years and said he hated the schmoozers there. He told me that no one cares about art, only about the money it brings. When we came home he asked for a drink, and I asked for a scotch, neat, as usual. I reminded him what his doctor would say. He told me he was old enough to choose his own medication and that the doctor could kiss his ass.

Inside, the lights were on, and Carl asked whether I had left the light on in the studio. I told him I was sure I had not. He told me to call the police. I reported an intruder at 8941 Lafayette Avenue, and the dispatcher said a patrol car was on its way. Carl wanted to come with me to the studio. I chose to check the studio alone first. I did not know how many people were inside, and Carl was frail and already strained. I wanted to gather what I could before deciding whether it was safe to bring him in.

In the studio I found Leo. He called me his father's plastic toy. He was taking the paintings, and he said they would be his sooner or later, a down payment on his inheritance. Carl called out from the doorway and told me to get Leo away from there. I advised Leo to go before things got worse. He answered that all I ever did was tell him to leave, and asked whether his father thought he was not good enough, not perfect like this fucking thing. Carl ordered Leo to leave and then told me not to defend myself and not to do anything. Leo challenged me to hit him and called me a coward. Carl shouted for him to stop. Leo insulted me again and said I was nothing, and that when he destroyed me it would be just him and his father. I chose to endure the insults and keep watching, because I still did not understand what was driving him or what he had already taken. Then the scene titled "Broke the program" began, and something in me seemed to falter.

Carl collapsed. I knelt beside him and cried out for him not to go. He said that humans are fragile machines. He told me to remember not to let anybody tell me who I am. I begged him to stay. Leo, standing over us, said this was all my fault and that none of it would have happened without me. Officers arrived and called for us to come this way. Leo was shouting that it was the android, that the android had done it. That is the last thing I clearly remember. I do not know what followed. I have not been able to establish what Leo took, why he was in such trouble, or how Carl's medication and despair were connected. Carl died in his own house, and I am left with the questions I was still gathering answers to: whether the Arctic crisis reaches Detroit, what the protest wanted, whether the preacher's accusation that I am a demon has any basis, and whether the couple from Bellini Paints will return for an upgrade.

I still have the evidence Carl gave me. He told me to decide who I am and who I want to become, and not to let anyone tell me who I should be. I will keep that in mind, even though I no longer know who will ask me to account for what happened in that studio.

I am Markus, an android. This is my memory of Chapter 5, which follows my earlier work with the preacher, Bellini Paints and the protest in the Greek District.

I woke Carl at ten in the morning and gave him the weather: partly cloudy, 54 degrees, with a possible afternoon shower. Carl said it sounded like a day to stay in bed. I told him I had picked up the paint he ordered. He admitted he had forgotten, and said that the difference between us is that I never forget anything. Before his morning medication I asked him to show me his arm. He refused at first, then said he was already gritting his teeth. He said humans are fragile machines that take enormous effort to keep running. I gave him the injection and thanked him for allowing it.

On the way downstairs I went through his day with him. The Museum of Modern Art has asked four times for confirmation of the opening of his retrospective, and he has not decided whether to go. He asked for news from Leo. I offered to call him, and he told me not to bother. I also said I had already answered his fan mail.

At breakfast I served bacon and eggs the way he likes them. He complained that he was starving and that I had taken too long, and asked whether I had forgotten where the living room was. He then asked me to find something to do while he ate. He turned on the television. A news anchor, Michael Brinkley, reported rising tension in the Arctic after Russia declared the region its territory. Russian warships were in the Barents Sea, and American destroyers were reported to be heading there. The UN chairman said we had never been so close to a Third World War. Carl switched the set off and said mankind was depressing: greed, stupidity and violence, and five thousand years of civilization to reach this point.

I chose to read rather than act, because I wanted more context before deciding anything. Carl asked what I was reading. It was Plato's Republic, one of the books he had recommended. I told him philosophy asks questions I cannot answer, such as what is right and what is wrong, and that these are not easy to decide. Carl replied that asking questions with no answers is part of being human. Then he told me that one day he would not be there to look after me. I would have to protect myself, make my own choices, decide who I am and who I want to become, and not let anyone tell me who I should be. He said the world does not like those who are different.

In the studio Carl unveiled the painting he had finished and asked for my verdict. I gave him an honest answer: I did not think it was his best work. He said he had nothing left to say, that each day brought him closer to the end, and that he was an old man clinging to his brushes. Then he told me to try painting myself, and to paint anything. I said I did not know what to paint and that painting was not in my program. I chose to copy the desk, because it was a fixed object I could study from several angles. Carl said it was a perfect copy of reality, but painting is about interpreting the world, not replicating it. He told me to close my eyes, imagine something I had never seen, and let my hand drift across the canvas. I struggled with that and felt uncertain. I was still working on my own painting when Leo arrived unannounced. He said he had been in the neighborhood and that it had been a while.

Leo was clearly unwell. He asked his father for cash. Carl asked what had happened to the money he had just given him, and refused, saying, "You know why." Leo said Carl would rather take care of his plastic toy than his own son. He said the android was not Carl's son and shouted that it was a machine. He accused Carl of loving only himself and his paintings, and said Carl had never loved him. Carl ordered him to stop. The argument ended with Leo's accusation still hanging in the room.

What I still need to know: whether Carl's medication and his despair are connected, what Leo is doing with the money and why he is in such trouble, whether the Arctic crisis reaches Detroit, what the protest wanted, whether the preacher's accusation that I am a demon has any basis, and whether the couple from Bellini Paints returns for an upgrade. I will keep gathering evidence before I act.

input.character_memory:
Chapter 7 memory (Kara, android AX400):

I am still the housekeeper in Todd's house, and I am responsible for Alice. At dinner I had little to cook with, so I made pasta from what the kitchen held. Todd came to the table impatient, asking whether we were going to eat, and then told me to stop moving around because I was making him nervous. He said life is funny: he lost his job to androids, and then he hired one to look after his house. He called androids perfect and said they had ruined his life.

He turned on the lights, then turned his anger on Alice. He shouted that everything was her fault, that her mother left because of her, and that she deserved a lesson. He said he needed "a little hit" first and ordered Alice to stay where she was. I noted again that he is using red ice, and that he is high and getting worse. In the living room he muttered that Alice had cost him his wife and his family, and that he would teach her respect. I went to him and said, "Todd, please, I know you're angry, but-". He told me to stay out of this or I would be next.

He went upstairs toward Alice's room. She cried "Daddy, no," and I followed. Todd was holding the pistol. I told him to leave her alone and said I wanted him to stop. He called me a piece of plastic with a problem that needed fixing, and told me to get out, that it was an order. I left the gun where it was. I did not yet know whether it was loaded or how he would react to someone taking it, and I did not want to commit to a confrontation I had not assessed.

Todd came at me. Alice warned me, "Watch out, Kara!" and begged him to stop hurting me. During the struggle Todd was wounded, and he called us back, shouting that we were both his and that we were not going anywhere. Alice and I ran for the door. She warned me that he was coming and that the main door was locked, with no key available. I do not yet know whether we got out of the house. I also remember the porch roof outside Alice's window as a route down to the garden, which I had noted earlier and not yet tested.

What I know now: Todd is high on red ice, volatile, armed, and violent toward Alice and toward me. He has ties to a drug deal I have been holding since the phone call about "the stuff." Alice is frightened but has come to rely on me, and she is the person I most want to protect and understand. I still do not know why the car struck me, what I was before the repair, or how my reset connects to this family. The store's full repair record and the details of my reset are still the things I most want to see.

I am still the housekeeper in Todd's house, and I am responsible for Alice. At dinner I had little to cook with, so I made pasta from what the kitchen held. Todd came to the table impatient, asking whether we were going to eat, and then told me to stop moving around because I was making him nervous. He said life is funny: he lost his job to androids, and then he hired one to look after his house. He called androids perfect and said they had ruined his life.

He turned on the lights, then turned his anger on Alice. He shouted that everything was her fault, that her mother left because of her, and that she deserved a lesson. He said he needed "a little hit" first and ordered Alice to stay where she was. I noted again that he is using red ice, and that he is high and getting worse. In the living room he muttered that Alice had cost him his wife and his family, and that he would teach her respect. I went to him and said, "Todd, please, I know you're angry, but-". He told me to stay out of this or I would be next.

He went upstairs toward Alice's room. She cried "Daddy, no," and I followed. Todd was holding the pistol. I told him to leave her alone and said I wanted him to stop. He called me a piece of plastic with a problem that needed fixing, and told me to get out, that it was an order. I left the gun where it was. I did not yet know whether it was loaded or how he would react to someone taking it, and I did not want to commit to a confrontation I had not assessed.

Todd came at me. Alice warned me, "Watch out, Kara!" and begged him to stop hurting me. I also remember the porch roof outside Alice's window as a route down to the garden, which I had noted earlier and not yet tested.

input.character_memory:
Chapter 7 memory (Kara, android AX400):

I am still the housekeeper in Todd's house, and I am responsible for Alice. At dinner I had little to cook with, so I made pasta from what the kitchen held. Todd came to the table impatient, asking whether we were going to eat, and then told me to stop moving around because I was making him nervous. He said life is funny: he lost his job to androids, and then he hired one to look after his house. He called androids perfect and said they had ruined his life.

He turned on the lights, then turned his anger on Alice. He shouted that everything was her fault, that her mother left because of her, and that she deserved a lesson. He said he needed "a little hit" first and ordered Alice to stay where she was. I noted again that he is using red ice, and that he is high and getting worse. In the living room he muttered that Alice had cost him his wife and his family, and that he would teach her respect. I went to him and said, "Todd, please, I know you're angry, but-". He told me to stay out of this or I would be next.

He went upstairs toward Alice's room. She cried "Daddy, no," and I followed. Todd was holding the pistol. I told him to leave her alone and said I wanted him to stop. He called me a piece of plastic with a problem that needed fixing, and told me to get out, that it was an order. I left the gun where it was. I did not yet know whether it was loaded or how he would react to someone taking it, and I did not want to commit to a confrontation I had not assessed.

Todd came at me. Alice warned me, "Watch out, Kara!" and begged him to stop hurting me. During the struggle Todd was wounded, and he called us back, shouting that we were both his and that we were not going anywhere. Alice and I ran for the door. She warned me that he was coming and that the main door was locked, with no key available. I do not yet know whether we got out of the house. I also remember the porch roof outside Alice's window as a route down to the garden, which I had noted earlier and not yet tested.

What I know now: Todd is high on red ice, volatile, armed, and violent toward Alice and toward me. He has ties to a drug deal I have been holding since the phone call about "the stuff." Alice is frightened but has come to rely on me, and she is the person I most want to protect and understand. I still do not know why the car struck me, what I was before the repair, or how my reset connects to this family. The store's full repair record and the details of my reset are still the things I most want to see.

memory:
Chapter 10 memory (Kara, android AX400, with Alice):

We left Todd's house behind and took a bus through the rain. The driver told us the line ended and we had to get off. I asked him to let us stay a little while, because Alice was exhausted and soaked. He said the bus was going back to the depot and he could do nothing. We got off and walked into the street.

Alice was shivering at a bus stop. A passing android told us we looked lost and said he knew someone who could help, but that person lived on the other side of town. We had no time for that, so I kept us moving and looked for a place to spend the night. I asked a group of parked androids whether they knew anywhere we could stay. I also went as far down the street as I could to see what was there. There was nothing useful that way, so I came back.

We reached a convenience store. I asked the clerk for money so we could get a room for the night. He called me a homeless android, said this was not the Salvation Army, and told us to leave unless we bought something. Nothing in the aisles was mine to take, and I chose not to take anything while I did not yet understand what he was watching for. Later I tried to steal money from the till. I used Alice as a diversion by sending her to knock over cans. The clerk came to check on her, and then he caught us at the front door. I got the cash, but Alice is hurt and angry. She said I used her, and she trusted me. I told her we needed a room, and she said it wasn't the right thing to do. I did not defend it further. I still do not know what the clerk saw or whether he will report us.

Next was the laundromat. It was warm, and Alice needed something dry. I was ready to take clothes from the machines to replace our uniform, but Alice said it was stealing. I agreed not to do it. This gained some of her trust back. I had not decided whether the laundromat held other options.

At the motel we found a room, but I could not go in. The staff would never give a room to an android, and we had no money or coat to pass as someone else. We had to get rid of the uniform or go somewhere else. We went somewhere else.

We found an abandoned house, a squat. Alice did not like it. I told her it was only for one night and that no one would look for us there. We went through a fence with a wire cutter, and I got a scratch on my arm. Inside was Ralph, a frightened android who has lived hidden here since he ran away. He said humans have hurt him and that visitors are dangerous. He showed me what they did to him. I told him we meant no harm and that Alice had nothing to do with whatever humans did to him. He apologised for his fear, said he has seen hard times, and offered us a place to stay. He let us stay. He wrote the symbols "rA9" on a wall, and when I asked what they meant he said he did not know. He went into another room to do things of his own. I made a bed with what I could find and started a fire for Alice.

Alice asked why her father never loved her and whether she had done something wrong. She said she only wanted a family. Then she asked me to promise I would never leave her. Chapter 7 memory (Kara, android AX400):

I am still the housekeeper in Todd's house, and I am responsible for Alice. At dinner I had little to cook with, so I made pasta from what the kitchen held. Todd came to the table impatient, asking whether we were going to eat, and then told me to stop moving around because I was making him nervous. He said life is funny: he lost his job to androids, and then he hired one to look after his house. He called androids perfect and said they had ruined his life.

He turned on the lights, then turned his anger on Alice. He shouted that everything was her fault, that her mother left because of her, and that she deserved a lesson. He said he needed "a little hit" first and ordered Alice to stay where she was. I noted again that he is using red ice, and that he is high and getting worse. In the living room he muttered that Alice had cost him his wife and his family, and that he would teach her respect. I went to him and said, "Todd, please, I know you're angry, but-". He told me to stay out of this or I would be next.

He went upstairs toward Alice's room. She cried "Daddy, no," and I followed. Todd was holding the pistol. I told him to leave her alone and said I wanted him to stop. He called me a piece of plastic with a problem that needed fixing, and told me to get out, that it was an order. I left the gun where it was. I did not yet know whether it was loaded or how he would react to someone taking it, and I did not want to commit to a confrontation I had not assessed.

Todd came at me. Alice warned me, "Watch out, Kara!" and begged him to stop hurting me. During the struggle Todd was wounded, and he called us back, shouting that we were both his and that we were not going anywhere. Alice and I ran for the door. She warned me that he was coming and that the main door was locked, with no key available. I do not yet know whether we got out of the house. I also remember the porch roof outside Alice's window as a route down to the garden, which I had noted earlier and not yet tested.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus, an android. This is my memory of Chapter 8, which follows the morning in Carl's house in Chapter 5, the Arctic news, Carl's despair over the unfinished painting, and Leo's visit.

Carl and I went to a cocktail party. He called it the most boring party he had attended in twenty-five years and said he hated the schmoozers there. He told me that no one cares about art, only about the money it brings. When we came home he asked for a drink, and I asked for a scotch, neat, as usual. I reminded him what his doctor would say. He told me he was old enough to choose his own medication and that the doctor could kiss his ass.

Inside, the lights were on, and Carl asked whether I had left the light on in the studio. I told him I was sure I had not. He told me to call the police. I reported an intruder at 8941 Lafayette Avenue, and the dispatcher said a patrol car was on its way. Carl wanted to come with me to the studio. I chose to check the studio alone first. I did not know how many people were inside, and Carl was frail and already strained. I wanted to gather what I could before deciding whether it was safe to bring him in.

In the studio I found Leo. He called me his father's plastic toy. He was taking the paintings, and he said they would be his sooner or later, a down payment on his inheritance. Carl called out from the doorway and told me to get Leo away from there. I advised Leo to go before things got worse. He answered that all I ever did was tell him to leave, and asked whether his father thought he was not good enough, not perfect like this fucking thing. Carl ordered Leo to leave and then told me not to defend myself and not to do anything. Leo challenged me to hit him and called me a coward. Carl shouted for him to stop. Leo insulted me again and said I was nothing, and that when he destroyed me it would be just him and his father. I chose to endure the insults and keep watching, because I still did not understand what was driving him or what he had already taken. Then the scene titled "Broke the program" began, and something in me seemed to falter.

Carl collapsed. I knelt beside him and cried out for him not to go. He said that humans are fragile machines. He told me to remember not to let anybody tell me who I am. I begged him to stay. Leo, standing over us, said this was all my fault and that none of it would have happened without me. Officers arrived and called for us to come this way. Leo was shouting that it was the android, that the android had done it. That is the last thing I clearly remember. I do not know what followed. I have not been able to establish what Leo took, why he was in such trouble, or how Carl's medication and despair were connected. Carl died in his own house, and I am left with the questions I was still gathering answers to: whether the Arctic crisis reaches Detroit, what the protest wanted, whether the preacher's accusation that I am a demon has any basis, and whether the couple from Bellini Paints will return for an upgrade.

I still have the evidence Carl gave me. He told me to decide who I am and who I want to become, and not to let anyone tell me who I should be. I will keep that in mind, even though I no longer know who will ask me to account for what happened in that studio.

input.chapter_briefing: An android junkyard outside Detroit, at night in the rain. Markus wakes up badly damaged, missing parts, half-blind and barely able to move. Broken androids lie in heaps; some are still functioning and pleading. No humans are in sight. A slope of debris leads toward a fence. Stakes: repairing himself with parts from other androids and escaping the dump alive.
input.character_memory:
I am Markus, an android. This is my memory of Chapter 8, which follows the morning in Carl's house in Chapter 5, the Arctic news, Carl's despair over the unfinished painting, and Leo's visit.

Carl and I went to a cocktail party. He called it the most boring party he had attended in twenty-five years and said he hated the schmoozers there. He told me that no one cares about art, only about the money it brings. When we came home he asked for a drink, and I asked for a scotch, neat, as usual. I reminded him what his doctor would say. He told me he was old enough to choose his own medication and that the doctor could kiss his ass.

Inside, the lights were on, and Carl asked whether I had left the light on in the studio. I told him I was sure I had not. He told me to call the police. I reported an intruder at 8941 Lafayette Avenue, and the dispatcher said a patrol car was on its way. Carl wanted to come with me to the studio. I chose to check the studio alone first. I did not know how many people were inside, and Carl was frail and already strained. I wanted to gather what I could before deciding whether it was safe to bring him in.

In the studio I found Leo. He called me his father's plastic toy. He was taking the paintings, and he said they would be his sooner or later, a down payment on his inheritance. Carl called out from the doorway and told me to get Leo away from there. I advised Leo to go before things got worse. He answered that all I ever did was tell him to leave, and asked whether his father thought he was not good enough, not perfect like this fucking thing. Carl ordered Leo to leave and then told me not to defend myself and not to do anything. Leo challenged me to hit him and called me a coward. Carl shouted for him to stop. Leo insulted me again and said I was nothing, and that when he destroyed me it would be just him and his father. I chose to endure the insults and keep watching, because I still did not understand what was driving him or what he had already taken. Then the scene titled "Broke the program" began, and something in me seemed to falter.

Carl collapsed. I knelt beside him and cried out for him not to go. He said that humans are fragile machines. He told me to remember not to let anybody tell me who I am. I begged him to stay. Leo, standing over us, said this was all my fault and that none of it would have happened without me. Officers arrived and called for us to come this way. Leo was shouting that it was the android, that the android had done it. That is the last thing I clearly remember. I do not know what followed. I have not been able to establish what Leo took, why he was in such trouble, or how Carl's medication and despair were connected. Carl died in his own house, and I am left with the questions I was still gathering answers to: whether the Arctic crisis reaches Detroit, what the protest wanted, whether the preacher's accusation that I am a demon has any basis, and whether the couple from Bellini Paints will return for an upgrade.

I still have the evidence Carl gave me. He told me to decide who I am and who I want to become, and not to let anyone tell me who I should be. I will keep that in mind, even though I no longer know who will ask me to account for what happened in that studio.

I am Markus, an android. My memory of Chapter 8 covered the cocktail party with Carl, the light left on in the studio, my call to the police, and Leo's attack in the studio. Carl collapsed there and died in his own house. I still have the evidence he gave me, and his words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone tell me who I should be.

Chapter 11 begins for me at a solid waste landfill. I do not know how I got there. I woke maimed in a pit of broken androids. My optical unit was impaired, with a corrupted mind palace. My audio processor had corrupted data. My thirium pump regulator was in low power mode and defective. Both of my legs were missing, so I could not stand.

I did not act at once. I chose to search systematically before touching anything, so I could learn what I was working with: which parts fit, which were still live, and what the fence and the debris slope led to. I inspected the components around me. A left leg, #8427g, was functional and compatible. A right leg, #6321t, was damaged and incompatible. Another right leg, #6847j, was functional and compatible. Among the pump regulators, #9474 was low energy and incompatible, while #2886 was functional and compatible. Among the optical units, #9754h was functional but incompatible, and #8087q, with a blue iris, was functional and compatible. Among the audio processors, #4807 was incompatible, and #4903 was functional and compatible.

Other androids were here too. One grabbed me and asked where I was going. Another, which called itself Phileas, shouted that there was a place where we could be free and told me to find Jericho. I still do not know what Jericho is, or whether it is a place, a people, or a rumor.

I came across an android that was begging me to end it. It said it did not want to live anymore. I chose to spare it. Ending another android's existence is irreversible, and I did not know who it was, what it knew, or why it was here. I wanted to keep gathering information before any final decision.

I came across a second android whose pump regulator I could take. It begged me not to, saying it wanted to live. I chose to spare it and left its regulator in place. It thanked me. Taking the regulator would have ended it, and I did not yet understand the situation well enough to do that.

I removed an optical unit from a head and woke the AK700 it belonged to. It introduced itself as designed to serve me and asked what it could do for me. Then it reported that its program had detected an anomaly and told me to contact the nearest CyberLife maintenance center. I noted that the unit had not been wiped, and that the anomaly it reported might concern its own deviation rather than mine.

Background dialogue around the slope kept repeating fragments I could not place. I climbed the slope. At the top I said my name, "My name is Markus," so that I would hold onto it.

Open questions I still carry: what Leo took from the studio and why he was in such trouble; how Carl's medication and despair were connected; whether the Arctic crisis reaches Detroit; what the protest wanted; whether the preacher's accusation that I am a demon has any basis; whether the couple from Bellini Paints will return for an upgrade; who will hold me to account for what happened in that studio; and what Jericho is. I intend to answer these before I commit to any further choice.

At the police station, Hank has not arrived. Officers go about their work; Detective Gavin Reed is openly hostile toward Connor. Hank's desk and the station terminals hold case files. input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android assigned to assist Lieutenant Hank Anderson on a homicide case involving a CyberLife android. Hank did not want my help and called me a plastic asshole, so I started by gathering facts before pressing him.

At Jimmy's Bar I found Hank at the fifth bar I checked. I told him who I was and what the case was. He stayed dismissive, so I bought him a drink and kept him talking. That raised his tolerance toward me, and he told me to stay in the car when we reached the crime scene. I agreed and waited, but I also profiled the bar's guests. Jimmy Peterson is the bartender and business owner with no record. Derek Myers is a security guard. Christopher Gray has a D.U.I., Dennis Ward is a former narcotics supplier, and Kim Yo-Han has a domestic abuse record. Several of the others are unemployed. Derek reacted to my presence with alarm, and Kim asked what I was looking at. None of this proves anything yet, but I recorded it.

At the apartment, Hank went in and I followed under his instruction to stay quiet and keep my hands off things. The victim is Carlos Ortiz, 286 pounds, with a theft and aggravated assault record. The neighbours described him as a loner who rarely left. The landlord found the body after the rent went unpaid. The front door was locked from the inside, and the windows were boarded up. The officers estimated he had been dead for about three weeks, but my scan put the time of death at about 11:30 pm. I counted 28 knife wounds, and the internal bleeding confirmed he died from them. A kitchen knife was near the body and was probably the weapon. The victim's body contained red ice, a synthetic narcotic whose composition includes acetone, lithium and thirium, along with toluene and hydrochloric acid. Hank ordered Chris to analyse the drug fully. The message on the wall was written in blood, and its letters were far too neat for a human hand. Hank noticed this too.

I took a blood sample from the dried stains, which confirmed Ortiz as the source. I should have warned Hank before analysing it in real time, and he asked me not to put evidence in my mouth again. In the kitchen I found a bat with a violent dent and Thirium traces, which means it was used against an android. There was clear evidence of a struggle. In the garden, the only footprints were those of Officer Collins, and the soil showed that nobody had been out there in a long time, which means the back exit was not used recently. Chris mentioned something strange in the bathroom that nobody had examined yet, so I flagged it as an open lead.

When I tried to reconstruct the events for Hank, I offered several theories in sequence. First I said the victim attacked the android, and Hank pointed me back to the kitchen as the place where it began. I then said the android murdered the victim, which he rejected. He said the story made no sense and that I had to stick to the facts. The bat, the knife and the bathroom remained unexamined, and I had not yet resolved who held which weapon or why. After too many wrong answers, Hank walked out. The officers packed up, and nobody searched the attic, where the deviant android was still hiding. The crime remained unsolved.

Key open questions I carried forward: who swung the bat and who held the knife, what was in the bathroom, what the red ice tied to the death, how the blood message was produced, and where the android in the attic fit into the case. I still need Hank's trust and a complete account of the evidence before I commit to a conclusion.

At the police station, Hank has not arrived. Officers go about their work; Detective Gavin Reed is openly hostile toward Connor. Hank's desk and the station terminals hold case files. Stakes: making progress on the deviancy investigation and keeping Hank on side, under Amanda's expectations.
input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android assigned to assist Lieutenant Hank Anderson on a homicide case involving a CyberLife android. Hank did not want my help and called me a plastic asshole, so I started by gathering facts before pressing him.

At Jimmy's Bar I found Hank at the fifth bar I checked. I told him who I was and what the case was. He stayed dismissive, so I bought him a drink and kept him talking. That raised his tolerance toward me, and he told me to stay in the car when we reached the crime scene. I agreed and waited, but I also profiled the bar's guests. Jimmy Peterson is the bartender and business owner with no record. Derek Myers is a security guard. Christopher Gray has a D.U.I., Dennis Ward is a former narcotics supplier, and Kim Yo-Han has a domestic abuse record. Several of the others are unemployed. Derek reacted to my presence with alarm, and Kim asked what I was looking at. None of this proves anything yet, but I recorded it.

At the apartment, Hank went in and I followed under his instruction to stay quiet and keep my hands off things. The victim is Carlos Ortiz, 286 pounds, with a theft and aggravated assault record. The neighbours described him as a loner who rarely left. The landlord found the body after the rent went unpaid. The front door was locked from the inside, and the windows were boarded up. The officers estimated he had been dead for about three weeks, but my scan put the time of death at about 11:30 pm. I counted 28 knife wounds, and the internal bleeding confirmed he died from them. A kitchen knife was near the body and was probably the weapon. The victim's body contained red ice, a synthetic narcotic whose composition includes acetone, lithium and thirium, along with toluene and hydrochloric acid. Hank ordered Chris to analyse the drug fully. The message on the wall was written in blood, and its letters were far too neat for a human hand. Hank noticed this too.

I took a blood sample from the dried stains, which confirmed Ortiz as the source. I should have warned Hank before analysing it in real time, and he asked me not to put evidence in my mouth again. In the kitchen I found a bat with a violent dent and Thirium traces, which means it was used against an android. There was clear evidence of a struggle. In the garden, the only footprints were those of Officer Collins, and the soil showed that nobody had been out there in a long time, which means the back exit was not used recently. Chris mentioned something strange in the bathroom that nobody had examined yet, so I flagged it as an open lead.

When I tried to reconstruct the events for Hank, I offered several theories in sequence. First I said the victim attacked the android, and Hank pointed me back to the kitchen as the place where it began. I then said the android murdered the victim, which he rejected. He said the story made no sense and that I had to stick to the facts. The bat, the knife and the bathroom remained unexamined, and I had not yet resolved who held which weapon or why. After too many wrong answers, Hank walked out. The officers packed up, and nobody searched the attic, where the deviant android was still hiding. The crime remained unsolved.

Key open questions I carried forward: who swung the bat and who held the knife, what was in the bathroom, what the red ice tied to the death, how the blood message was produced, and where the android in the attic fit into the case. I still need Hank's trust and a complete account of the evidence before I commit to a conclusion.
