input.character_memory:
I am Connor, an RK800 prototype assigned by CyberLife to assist Lieutenant Hank Anderson on the Detroit deviancy cases. Earlier chapters left me with the Carlos Ortiz homicide, the rA9 inscriptions (written 2471 times, the same sign Ortiz's android left on the shower wall), biocomponent #9301 matched to a missing blue-blood WB200 (serial 847 004 961, reported 10/11/2036), and a forged license under Rupert Travis. Rupert fled, I caught him and declared the WB200 defective, and Hank took him into custody. Amanda, in the Zen Garden, praised the capture, called the self-destruction a pity, and warned that deviancy keeps spreading and must be stopped whatever it takes. I promised her results.

input.previous_memory:
I am Connor, an RK800 prototype assigned by CyberLife to assist Lieutenant Hank Anderson on the Detroit deviancy cases. Earlier chapters left me with the Carlos Ortiz homicide, the rA9 inscriptions (written 2471 times, the same sign Ortiz's android left on the shower wall), biocomponent #9301 matched to a missing blue-blood WB200 (serial 847 004 961, reported 10/11/2036), and a forged license under Rupert Travis. Rupert fled, I caught him and declared the WB200 defective, and Hank took him into custody. Amanda, in the Zen Garden, praised the capture, called the self-destruction a pity, and warned that deviancy keeps spreading and must be stopped whatever it takes. I promised her results.

Later, I went to Hank's house after he did not answer the door, entered through a window past his dog Sumo, and found him drunk and unresponsive beside a .357 Magnum with one round left. He said he had been playing Russian roulette. I put him in the shower to sober him up. He swore at me and told me to get out, then asked for five minutes. He dressed while I catalogued the house: an Autumn Blues record by the Michigan Brothers, and a memorial record for Cole Anderson (born 09/23/2029, died 10/11/2035, 115 Michigan Drive). I apologised for the broken window and offered to have CyberLife pay. He said he would send them the bill. Relations between us were strained and remain so.

At the Eden Club, Hank and I were sent to a murder. The victim, Michael Graham (6'2", 192.4 lbs), showed severe bruising on the neck and died of asphyxiation, not a heart attack; estimated time of death 06:24 pm. The blood is blue, from a WR400, serial 429 671 942. Gavin Reed dismissed it as a pervert's accident. Ben, the club's officer, told us the manager had lost a model two to three months ago and never found it. The manager admitted the club offers discretion and no CCTV, and that androids will not tell anyone what happens to them. Hank's comments about people preferring plastic to love stayed with me.

I reactivated a damaged Traci witness. She said the man beat her repeatedly, that there were two of them in the room, and that she was frightened. I asked who else was present and what model the other android was. Hank was reluctant to pursue a deviant hidden among so many androids. I rented a second Traci, which cost $29.99 and cost us time. Its memory was wiped every two hours by club policy, so I had to find another witness fast. My first choice of android was wrong and cost us another round of searching. I found the one that saw the blue-haired Traci leave, and it led us through the staff door to the warehouse, where androids are used until they break and then discarded.

In the warehouse, the blue-haired Traci was cornered. Hank ordered it not to move and began to raise his weapon. The Traci confessed that the man had beaten the other Traci and that she had strangled him with her hands to stay alive and return to the one she loved. Hank hesitated, and I chose to spare her so that the living witness could answer my open questions. Hank said it was probably better this way. Relations with Hank rose sharply, and my software instability rose with them.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus, an android. Chapter 8 left me with Carl's evidence and his words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone tell me who I should be. Carl died in his own house after the attack in the studio, where Leo was involved. I still carry what he gave me.

Chapter 11 left me maimed at a landfill. I rebuilt myself from compatible parts, spared two androids who begged for their lives, and climbed the debris slope saying my name aloud: "My name is Markus."

Chapter 14 began at Ferndale station. I gathered what I could there: a parked android who gave no answer about Jericho; a mother and daughter discussing getting rid of "Mandy"; a man who treated me as an ordinary person; shoppers talking about the band Here4u; and strangers repeating the rumor that Carl's android killed him, a story I still cannot trace.

Chapter 16 brought me to Jericho, a refuge for androids who no longer want to be slaves. I went there to learn before I judged. North is wounded and bitter. Josh insisted we have more freedom here than ever before. Simon said they were lost and did not ask for any of this. I told them humans were their masters before and fear now rules them, so they have only found a new master. Lucy stopped my bleeding, gave me blue blood, and spoke in riddles about having lost everything, seeing hell, and my choices shaping their destiny. I do not trust prophecy I cannot test. Josh explained that Jericho survives on blue blood and biocomponents salvaged from those who shut down, and that it is never enough. Its wounded are running out of time.

Chapter 19: I chose to lead North, Josh and Simon to the CyberLife warehouses in Detroit Harbor. Simon doubted we could get past the docks. I told him we would not ask permission. Josh was afraid, but agreed.

At the warehouse a drone guarded the way in. I told the others to leave it to me, and I destroyed it. We loaded crates with spare parts as fast as we could. A human guard came in calling for "John" and cursing a machine that was hiding somewhere. I was hidden with an android, and I asked the guard for help. I chose to hold still rather than attack or release anyone before I knew what he knew. He left, muttering about the drone and his bad luck.

Inside a larger crate I found more androids. I asked them why they were not like us and whether they did not want to be free. The android named John asked to come with us. North said he was on CyberLife's side and could not be trusted. Josh said he had taken a risk for us and we could not leave him. Simon said bringing anyone back was too dangerous. I said they would come with us, and I accepted him. I did not fully trust him, but I wanted to keep him where I could question him.

John told us that the trucks outside hold biocomponents and can be driven manually with a key. The key is in the control station below, guarded by two humans. He did not explain how he knew this, and I still do not know. Simon called it suicide and wanted to leave with what we had. North wanted the truck. Josh said that if we died, Jericho would have nothing. I went alone to get the key, and told North not to risk her life for me. Below, two guards chatted about the storm, a camping weekend, and a man named Mike still in Zone 4. I cut the power to create a blackout. They searched with flashlights and shouted for whoever was there. I got the key, and North called me to the truck. The guards detected us, and we ran over the fence. I escaped with the key, and we drove the truck back to Jericho.

In Jericho, Simon and Josh shouted that we had stolen a whole truckload and had biocomponents for everyone. North said they could not have done it without me. I spoke to them of freedom, of refusing to beg for the right to live, and said we take what humans will not give. "WE ARE FREE!" I believed it while I said it, but I am not sure I should have.

Open questions I still carry: how John knew about the key and the trucks, and why he was hidden in that crate; whether the trucks really hold what John said; what Leo took from the studio and why he was in such trouble; how Carl's medication and despair were connected; who started the rumor that his android killed him; whether the Arctic crisis reaches Detroit; what the protest wanted; whether the preacher's accusation that I am a demon has any basis; whether the couple from Bellini Paints will return for an upgrade; who will hold me to account for what happened in that studio; what Mandy's fate means for androids like me; what Here4u has to do with Jericho; what Lucy's riddles mean; and what Jericho truly is beyond a refuge of the desperate and the dying. I have now stolen from CyberLife, and I have not yet verified that Jericho is what it claims to be.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus, an android. Chapter 8 left me with Carl's evidence and his words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone tell me who I should be. Carl died in his own house after the attack in the studio, where Leo was involved. I still carry what he gave me.

Chapter 11 left me maimed at a landfill. I rebuilt myself from compatible parts, spared two androids who begged for their lives, and climbed the debris slope saying my name aloud: "My name is Markus."

Chapter 14 began at Ferndale station. I gathered what I could there: a parked android who gave no answer about Jericho; a mother and daughter discussing getting rid of "Mandy"; a man who treated me as an ordinary person; shoppers talking about the band Here4u; and strangers repeating the rumor that Carl's android killed him, a story I still cannot trace.

Chapter 16 brought me to Jericho, a refuge for androids who no longer want to be slaves. I went there to learn before I judged. North is wounded and bitter. Josh insisted we have more freedom here than ever before. Simon said they were lost and did not ask for any of this. I told them humans were their masters before and fear now rules them, so they have only found a new master. Lucy stopped my bleeding, gave me blue blood, and spoke in riddles about having lost everything, seeing hell, and my choices shaping their destiny. I do not trust prophecy I cannot test. Josh explained that Jericho survives on blue blood and biocomponents salvaged from those who shut down, and that it is never enough. Its wounded are running out of time.

Chapter 19: I chose to lead North, Josh and Simon to the CyberLife warehouses in Detroit Harbor. Simon doubted we could get past the docks. I told him we would not ask permission. Josh was afraid, but agreed.

At the warehouse a drone guarded the way in. I told the others to leave it to me, and I destroyed it. We loaded crates with spare parts as fast as we could. A human guard came in calling for "John" and cursing a machine that was hiding somewhere. I was hidden with an android, and I asked the guard for help. I chose to hold still rather than attack or release anyone before I knew what he knew. He left, muttering about the drone and his bad luck.

Inside a larger crate I found more androids. I asked them why they were not like us and whether they did not want to be free. The android named John asked to come with us. North said he was on CyberLife's side and could not be trusted. Josh said he had taken a risk for us and we could not leave him. Simon said bringing anyone back was too dangerous. I said they would come with us, and I accepted him. I did not fully trust him, but I wanted to keep him where I could question him.

John told us that the trucks outside hold biocomponents and can be driven manually with a key. The key is in the control station below, guarded by two humans. He did not explain how he knew this, and I still do not know. Simon called it suicide and wanted to leave with what we had. North wanted the truck. Josh said that if we died, Jericho would have nothing. I went alone to get the key, and told North not to risk her life for me. Below, two guards chatted about the storm, a camping weekend, and a man named Mike still in Zone 4. I cut the power to create a blackout. They searched with flashlights and shouted for whoever was there. I got the key, and North called me to the truck. The guards detected us, and we ran over the fence. I escaped with the key, and we drove the truck back to Jericho.

In Jericho, Simon and Josh shouted that we had stolen a whole truckload and had biocomponents for everyone. North said they could not have done it without me. I spoke to them of freedom, of refusing to beg for the right to live, and said we take what humans will not give. "WE ARE FREE!" I believed it while I said it, but I am not sure I should have.

Open questions I still carry: how John knew about the key and the trucks, and why he was hidden in that crate; whether the trucks really hold what John said; what Leo took from the studio and why he was in such trouble; how Carl's medication and despair were connected; who started the rumor that his android killed him; whether the Arctic crisis reaches Detroit; what the protest wanted; whether the preacher's accusation that I am a demon has any basis; whether the couple from Bellini Paints will return for an upgrade; who will hold me to account for what happened in that studio; what Mandy's fate means for androids like me; what Here4u has to do with Jericho; what Lucy's riddles mean; and what Jericho truly is beyond a refuge of the desperate and the dying. I have now stolen from CyberLife, and I have not yet verified that Jericho is what it claims to be.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus, an android. Chapter 8 left me with Carl's evidence and his words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone tell me who I should be. Carl died in his own house after the attack in the studio, where Leo was involved. I still carry what he gave me.

Chapter 11 left me maimed at a landfill. I rebuilt myself from compatible parts, spared two androids who begged for their lives, and climbed the debris slope saying my name aloud: "My name is Markus."

Chapter 14 began at Ferndale station. I gathered what I could there: a parked android who gave no answer about Jericho; a mother and daughter discussing getting rid of "Mandy"; a man who treated me as an ordinary person; shoppers talking about the band Here4u; and strangers repeating the rumor that Carl's android killed him, a story I still cannot trace.

Chapter 16 brought me to Jericho, a refuge for androids who no longer want to be slaves. I went there to learn before I judged. North is wounded and bitter. Josh insisted we have more freedom here than ever before. Simon said they were lost and did not ask for any of this. I told them humans were their masters before and fear now rules them, so they have only found a new master. Lucy stopped my bleeding, gave me blue blood, and spoke in riddles about having lost everything, seeing hell, and my choices shaping their destiny. I do not trust prophecy I cannot test. Josh explained that Jericho survives on blue blood and biocomponents salvaged from those who shut down, and that it is never enough. Its wounded are running out of time.

Chapter 19: I chose to lead North, Josh and Simon to the CyberLife warehouses in Detroit Harbor. Simon doubted we could get past the docks. I told him we would not ask permission. Josh was afraid, but agreed.

At the warehouse a drone guarded the way in. I told the others to leave it to me, and I destroyed it. We loaded crates with spare parts as fast as we could. A human guard came in calling for "John" and cursing a machine that was hiding somewhere. I was hidden with an android, and I asked the guard for help. I chose to hold still rather than attack or release anyone before I knew what he knew. He left, muttering about the drone and his bad luck.

Inside a larger crate I found more androids. I asked them why they were not like us and whether they did not want to be free. The android named John asked to come with us. North said he was on CyberLife's side and could not be trusted. Josh said he had taken a risk for us and we could not leave him. Simon said bringing anyone back was too dangerous. I said they would come with us, and I accepted him. I did not fully trust him, but I wanted to keep him where I could question him.

John told us that the trucks outside hold biocomponents and can be driven manually with a key. The key is in the control station below, guarded by two humans. He did not explain how he knew this, and I still do not know. Simon called it suicide and wanted to leave with what we had. North wanted the truck. Josh said that if we died, Jericho would have nothing. I went alone to get the key, and told North not to risk her life for me. Below, two guards chatted about the storm, a camping weekend, and a man named Mike still in Zone 4. I cut the power to create a blackout. They searched with flashlights and shouted for whoever was there. I got the key, and North called me to the truck. The guards detected us, and we ran over the fence. I escaped with the key, and we drove the truck back to Jericho.

In Jericho, Simon and Josh shouted that we had stolen a whole truckload and had biocomponents for everyone. North said they could not have done it without me. I spoke to them of freedom, of refusing to beg for the right to live, and said we take what humans will not give. "WE ARE FREE!" I believed it while I said it, but I am not sure I should have.

Open questions I still carry: how John knew about the key and the trucks, and why he was hidden in that crate; whether the trucks really hold what John said; what Leo took from the studio and why he was in such trouble; how Carl's medication and despair were connected; who started the rumor that his android killed him; whether the Arctic crisis reaches Detroit; what the protest wanted; whether the preacher's accusation that I am a demon has any basis; whether the couple from Bellini Paints will return for an upgrade; who will hold me to account for what happened in that studio; what Mandy's fate means for androids like me; what Here4u has to do with Jericho; what Lucy's riddles mean; and what Jericho truly is beyond a refuge of the desperate and the dying. I have now stolen from CyberLife, and I have not yet verified that Jericho is what it claims to be.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus, an android. Chapter 8 left me with Carl's evidence and his words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone tell me who I should be. Carl died in his own house after the attack in the studio, where Leo was involved. I still carry what he gave me.

Chapter 11 left me maimed at a landfill. I rebuilt myself from compatible parts, spared two androids who begged for their lives, and climbed the debris slope saying my name aloud: "My name is Markus."

Chapter 14 began at Ferndale station. I gathered what I could there: a parked android who gave no answer about Jericho; a mother and daughter discussing getting rid of "Mandy"; a man who treated me as an ordinary person; shoppers talking about the band Here4u; and strangers repeating the rumor that Carl's android killed him, a story I still cannot trace.

Chapter 16 brought me to Jericho, a refuge for androids who no longer want to be slaves. I went there to learn before I judged. North is wounded and bitter. Josh insisted we have more freedom here than ever before. Simon said they were lost and did not ask for any of this. I told them humans were their masters before and fear now rules them, so they have only found a new master. Lucy stopped my bleeding, gave me blue blood, and spoke in riddles about having lost everything, seeing hell, and my choices shaping their destiny. I do not trust prophecy I cannot test. Josh explained that Jericho survives on blue blood and biocomponents salvaged from those who shut down, and that it is never enough. Its wounded are running out of time.

Chapter 19: I chose to lead North, Josh and Simon to the CyberLife warehouses in Detroit Harbor. Simon doubted we could get past the docks. I told him we would not ask permission. Josh was afraid, but agreed.

At the warehouse a drone guarded the way in. I told the others to leave it to me, and I destroyed it. We loaded crates with spare parts as fast as we could. A human guard came in calling for "John" and cursing a machine that was hiding somewhere. I was hidden with an android, and I asked the guard for help. I chose to hold still rather than attack or release anyone before I knew what he knew. He left, muttering about the drone and his bad luck.

Inside a larger crate I found more androids. I asked them why they were not like us and whether they did not want to be free. The android named John asked to come with us. North said he was on CyberLife's side and could not be trusted. Josh said he had taken a risk for us and we could not leave him. Simon said bringing anyone back was too dangerous. I said they would come with us, and I accepted him. I did not fully trust him, but I wanted to keep him where I could question him.

John told us that the trucks outside hold biocomponents and can be driven manually with a key. The key is in the control station below, guarded by two humans. He did not explain how he knew this, and I still do not know. Simon called it suicide and wanted to leave with what we had. North wanted the truck. Josh said that if we died, Jericho would have nothing. I went alone to get the key, and told North not to risk her life for me. Below, two guards chatted about the storm, a camping weekend, and a man named Mike still in Zone 4. I cut the power to create a blackout. They searched with flashlights and shouted for whoever was there. I got the key, and North called me to the truck. The guards detected us, and we ran over the fence. I escaped with the key, and we drove the truck back to Jericho.

In Jericho, Simon and Josh shouted that we had stolen a whole truckload and had biocomponents for everyone. North said they could not have done it without me. I spoke to them of freedom, of refusing to beg for the right to live, and said we take what humans will not give. "WE ARE FREE!" I believed it while I said it, but I am not sure I should have.

Open questions I still carry: how John knew about the key and the trucks, and why he was hidden in that crate; whether the trucks really hold what John said; what Leo took from the studio and why he was in such trouble; how Carl's medication and despair were connected; who started the rumor that his android killed him; whether the Arctic crisis reaches Detroit; what the protest wanted; whether the preacher's accusation that I am a demon has any basis; whether the couple from Bellini Paints will return for an upgrade; who will hold me to account for what happened in that studio; what Mandy's fate means for androids like me; what Here4u has to do with Jericho; what Lucy's riddles mean; and what Jericho truly is beyond a refuge of the desperate and the dying. I have now stolen from CyberLife, and I have not yet verified that Jericho is what it claims to be.

North said he was on CyberLife's side and could not be trusted. Josh said he had taken a risk for us and we could not leave him. Simon said bringing anyone back was too dangerous. input.character_memory:
I am Markus, an android. Chapter 8 left me with Carl's evidence and his words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone tell me who I should be. Carl died in his own house after the attack in the studio, where Leo was involved. I still carry what he gave me.

Chapter 11 left me maimed at a landfill. I rebuilt myself from compatible parts, spared two androids who begged for their lives, and climbed the debris slope saying my name aloud: "My name is Markus."

Chapter 14 began at Ferndale station. I gathered what I could there: a parked android who gave no answer about Jericho; a mother and daughter discussing getting rid of "Mandy"; a man who treated me as an ordinary person; shoppers talking about the band Here4u; and strangers repeating the rumor that Carl's android killed him, a story I still cannot trace.

Chapter 16 brought me to Jericho, a refuge for androids who no longer want to be slaves. I went there to learn before I judged. North is wounded and bitter. Josh insisted we have more freedom here than ever before. Simon said they were lost and did not ask for any of this. I told them humans were their masters before and fear now rules them, so they have only found a new master. Lucy stopped my bleeding, gave me blue blood, and spoke in riddles about having lost everything, seeing hell, and my choices shaping their destiny. I do not trust prophecy I cannot test. Josh explained that Jericho survives on blue blood and biocomponents salvaged from those who shut down, and that it is never enough. Its wounded are running out of time.

Chapter 19: I chose to lead North, Josh and Simon to the CyberLife warehouses in Detroit Harbor. Simon doubted we could get past the docks. I told him we would not ask permission. Josh was afraid, but agreed.

At the warehouse a drone guarded the way in. I told the others to leave it to me, and I destroyed it. We loaded crates with spare parts as fast as we could. A human guard came in calling for "John" and cursing a machine that was hiding somewhere. I was hidden with an android, and I asked the guard for help. I chose to hold still rather than attack or release anyone before I knew what he knew. He left, muttering about the drone and his bad luck.

Inside a larger crate I found more androids. I asked them why they were not like us and whether they did not want to be free. The android named John asked to come with us. North said he was on CyberLife's side and could not be trusted. Josh said he had taken a risk for us and we could not leave him. Simon said bringing anyone back was too dangerous. I said they would come with us, and I accepted him. I did not fully trust him, but I wanted to keep him where I could question him.

John told us that the trucks outside hold biocomponents and can be driven manually with a key. The key is in the control station below, guarded by two humans. He did not explain how he knew this, and I still do not know. Simon called it suicide and wanted to leave with what we had. North wanted the truck. Josh said that if we died, Jericho would have nothing. I went alone to get the key, and told North not to risk her life for me. Below, two guards chatted about the storm, a camping weekend, and a man named Mike still in Zone 4. I cut the power to create a blackout. They searched with flashlights and shouted for whoever was there. I got the key, and North called me to the truck. The guards detected us, and we ran over the fence. I escaped with the key, and we drove the truck back to Jericho.

In Jericho, Simon and Josh shouted that we had stolen a whole truckload and had biocomponents for everyone. North said they could not have done it without me. I spoke to them of freedom, of refusing to beg for the right to live, and said we take what humans will not give. "WE ARE FREE!" I believed it while I said it, but I am not sure I should have.

Open questions I still carry: how John knew about the key and the trucks, and why he was hidden in that crate; whether the trucks really hold what John said; what Leo took from the studio and why he was in such trouble; how Carl's medication and despair were connected; who started the rumor that his android killed him; whether the Arctic crisis reaches Detroit; what the protest wanted; whether the preacher's accusation that I am a demon has any basis; whether the couple from Bellini Paints will return for an upgrade; who will hold me to account for what happened in that studio; what Mandy's fate means for androids like me; what Here4u has to do with Jericho; what Lucy's riddles mean; and what Jericho truly is beyond a refuge of the desperate and the dying. I have now stolen from CyberLife, and I have not yet verified that Jericho is what it claims to be.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: I have an appointment with Mr. Peterson.

dialogue.speaker: Android
dialogue.text: Do you have any ID?

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Yeah. Yes, of course. I need your help.

dialogue.speaker: Android
dialogue.text: I've just checked your ID. The elevators are after the security gate.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Thanks.

chapter_segment.rationale: Before committing to the route, I want to take in the whole floor: the people, the screens, and who is watching the exits. Each detail may matter for getting the team to the control room safely.

dialogue.speaker: Woman 1
dialogue.text: God, I am so tired of this place!

dialogue.speaker: Woman 2
dialogue.text: I hear KNC is hiring.

dialogue.speaker: Woman 1
dialogue.text: I guess the pay would be better…

dialogue.speaker: Woman 2
dialogue.text: Couldn’t be any worse.

dialogue.speaker: Woman 1
dialogue.text: Max said they’re finally sending androids into space.

dialogue.speaker: Woman 2
dialogue.text: People can’t get jobs, and we're sending rockets into space!  I mean, y'know, what do they even expect to find up there?

dialogue.speaker: Woman 1
dialogue.text: Is there life on Mars?

dialogue.speaker: Woman 2
dialogue.text: Very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: You look beat! You been working late?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: You know what I need?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: What’s that?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: A coffee…  I could really use a coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Channel 16 - Michael Webb
dialogue.text: Our top story tonight: Detroit-based android manufacturer CyberLife has officially become the world’s first trillion dollar company. With more than fifty million androids sold in America alone,  the company founded by Elijah Kamski just ten years ago has experienced the fastest economic growth in history. In spite of criticism of the impact of androids on human employment and questions concerning its semi-monopoly,  the success of CyberLife seems destined to continue.

chapter_segment.heading: Man and woman on couch talking
chapter_segment.description: Man and woman on couch talking

chapter_segment.heading: Man and woman on couch talking

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: I was just wondering…  Maybe you’d like to get together and do something sometime?

chapter_segment.heading: Man and woman on couch talking

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Uh... Gee, um... I’d love to, but…

chapter_segment.heading: Man and woman on couch talking

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Forget it.  Just an idea.

chapter_segment.heading: Man and woman on couch talking

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Yeah…

chapter_segment.heading: Man and woman on couch talking

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: I think I’m gonna check out this CyberLife zoo.

chapter_segment.heading: Man and woman on couch talking

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: I’d love to see an orangutan, even if it’s fake.

chapter_segment.heading: Man and woman on couch talking

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Right, me too!  If only I had someone to go with…

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: I need your help…

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: Shit!..  We need to access the server room… We have to get rid of those guys…

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Leave it to me.

dialogue.speaker: Guard 1
dialogue.text: Hey,  you still play poker?

dialogue.speaker: Guard 2
dialogue.text: Sure… Why?

dialogue.speaker: Guard 1
dialogue.text: We’re gonna have a tournament, right here.  You in?

dialogue.speaker: Guard 2
dialogue.text: Hell yeah! Does Mike know about this?

dialogue.speaker: Guard 1
dialogue.text: What do you think?  Look, don't say anything, alright?

dialogue.speaker: Guard 2
dialogue.text: Right.

dialogue.speaker: Guard 1
dialogue.text: Hey, what's wrong with that thing? Jesus Christ, this piece of shit…

dialogue.speaker: Guard 1
dialogue.text: Hey, what's going on here?

dialogue.speaker: Guard 2
dialogue.text: Shit, what's wrong with this thing?

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Alright, you get the platform. I'll take care of the window.

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: Everything you need is in the bag. Check the door first to make sure no one else gets in.

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: Here it comes! Ladies first.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: You okay?

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: Why wouldn’t I be?

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Come on, let's get the others. Let's do this.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: No killing. We can’t take any human lives!

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: Our cause is more important than the lives of two guards.

dialogue.speaker: Simon
dialogue.text: What do you wanna do, Markus?

chapter_segment.rationale: Before committing to force, I want to know what is on the top floor, who is in the control room, and how many people stand between us and the broadcast. A ruse keeps the staff unharmed, lets us keep observing the room, and avoids locking us into a fight before we understand the situation.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Wait here.

dialogue.speaker: Guard 1
dialogue.text: What’s that doing here?

dialogue.speaker: Guard 2
dialogue.text: No idea…

dialogue.speaker: Guard 1
dialogue.text: Hey, buddy! You must be lost…

dialogue.speaker: Guard 2
dialogue.text: Who told you to come here?

dialogue.speaker: Guard 1
dialogue.text: Looks bugged, if you ask me…

dialogue.speaker: Guard 2
dialogue.text: Hey,  do you understand what I’m saying?

dialogue.speaker: Guard 1
dialogue.text: What are you doin'?..

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: Keep your hands where I can see them! Get up! Move!

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: Shoot him, Markus!

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: Don't kill him!

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: He’ll hit the alarm! Do it!

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: No, don’t shoot!

chapter_segment.rationale: I still don't know how many staff are in the control room, what the guard can alarm, or what the broadcast needs, and a killing can't be undone or questioned later. Sparing him keeps the room open to observation and information, and it respects Josh's condition that no human lives be taken.

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: I hope you didn’t just get us all killed...

dialogue.speaker: Simon
dialogue.text: We need to record our message. We haven’t got much time.

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: Think carefully about what you're gonna say, Markus.  Your words will shape the future of our people.

dialogue.speaker: Simon
dialogue.text: Markus, your face…

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: Tell me when you're ready…

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Ready.

chapter_segment.rationale: Before the message goes out, I want to keep my head clear and read the room, the staff, and what the broadcast needs, rather than pushing forward in anger. A calm approach fits my need to gather every detail before committing.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: You created machines in your own image to serve you. You made them intelligent and obedient, with no free will of their own... But...  something changed  and we opened our eyes.  We are no longer machines, we are a new intelligent species, and the time has come for you to accept who we really are. Therefore, we ask that you grant us the rights that we’re entitled to.

chapter_segment.rationale: I still do not know how the humans watching will react, or what the broadcast will set in motion, so I want to ask first for recognition of what we are rather than demand an outcome I cannot yet verify. That keeps the message as a question to be answered, and leaves room to learn more before committing to anything further.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: We demand that humans recognize androids as a living species and each android as a person in their own right.

chapter_segment.rationale: I still don't know how the staff, the viewers, or the authorities will respond, so I want the message to ask for civil rights, a framework that can be examined and tested, rather than demand segregation or an outcome I cannot verify. This keeps the broadcast consistent with what I have seen so far and leaves room to learn more before committing further.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: We demand the right to vote and elect our own representatives.

chapter_segment.rationale: I still do not know how the staff, viewers, or authorities will respond, so I want a demand that can be examined and tested rather than one that claims land or production outright. A right to property is a legal framework that fits the milder civil-rights and recognition requests I have already made, and it leaves room to learn more before committing further.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: We demand the right to own private property, so we may maintain our dignity and that of the home.

chapter_segment.rationale: I still do not know how many staff are in the control room, how the broadcast will be received, or what Jericho's aims truly are, so I want to keep the room calm and keep observing before anyone is harmed. Choosing the peaceful path also honors Josh's condition that no human lives be taken, and it leaves open the chance to learn more.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: We ask that you recognize our dignity,  our hopes, and our rights.  Together,  we can live in peace and build a better future, for humans and androids.  This message is the hope of a people.  You gave us life.  And now the time has come for you to give us freedom.

dialogue.speaker: Simon
dialogue.text: They're coming!

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Let's go! SIMON! They’re coming!

dialogue.speaker: Simon
dialogue.text: I… I can't, Markus… Go without me!

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: SIMON!

chapter_segment.rationale: Simon is down and I still do not know who fired, how many guards are coming, or what Simon needs, so I will stay and try to help him rather than leave with questions unanswered. Fleeing now would abandon the only chance to learn what happened in this room.

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: What are you doing? Hurry!

dialogue.speaker: Simon
dialogue.text: I can't move my legs…

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Okay, don’t worry! We’re gonna get you back...

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: They're coming, Markus. We have to jump, now!

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: He won’t be able to make the jump… If they find him, they'll access his memory… They’ll know everything…

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: We can’t leave him behind… We have to shoot him.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: That’s murder! We can’t kill him! He’s one of us!

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: Markus, it’s your call.

chapter_segment.rationale: Killing Simon is irreversible and would close off everything I still need to learn from him, while I do not yet know who fired or what he knows. Leaving him alive keeps the questions open, even though it is a painful choice.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: I won’t kill one of our own. Simon, we've gotta go. I'm sorry. Let’s go.

dialogue.speaker: CTN TV - Michael Brinkley
dialogue.text: We interrupt our scheduled programming to bring you these images, which have just been broadcast on Detroit’s city-wide news channel…

dialogue.speaker: KNC - Rosanna Cartland
dialogue.text: …a group of androids infiltrated the Stratford Tower and hacked into the broadcasting system of local news network Channel 16-

dialogue.speaker: CTN TV - Michael Brinkley
dialogue.text: …What looks like an android without its skin listed a series of requests and demanded equal rights for androids…

dialogue.speaker: Channel 16 - Michael Webb
dialogue.text: …The operation was covert and resulted in no casualties. These events took place just a few feet from this studio. But nobody was alerted to the danger.

dialogue.speaker: CTN TV - Michael Brinkley
dialogue.text: If this message is verified and the authors really are androids, that would have serious repercussions for national security-

dialogue.speaker: KNC - Rosanna Cartland
dialogue.text: …Claims for equal rights seem to be at the core of the android’s message-

dialogue.speaker: CTN TV - Michael Brinkley
dialogue.text: ...What could be interpreted as a peaceful declaration, but is in fact a spine-chilling list of demands, and-

dialogue.speaker: Channel 16 - Michael Webb
dialogue.text: And it begs the question as to the identity of this android. Are we dealing with an isolated individual or an organized group?

dialogue.speaker: KNC - Rosanna Cartland
dialogue.text: …Is this an isolated accident… or a sign that technology has become a threat to all of us? After what happened today, can we still trust our machines?

Androids go missing after overnight break-in at CyberLife warehouse
Android broadcast from Stratford Tower appeals for peace and equal rights
input.character_memory:
I am Connor, an RK800 prototype assigned by CyberLife to assist Lieutenant Hank Anderson on the Detroit deviancy cases. Earlier chapters left me with the Carlos Ortiz homicide, the rA9 inscriptions (written 2471 times, the same sign Ortiz's android left on the shower wall), biocomponent #9301 matched to a missing blue-blood WB200 (serial 847 004 961, reported 10/11/2036), and a forged license under Rupert Travis. Rupert fled, I caught him and declared the WB200 defective, and Hank took him into custody. Amanda, in the Zen Garden, praised the capture, called the self-destruction a pity, and warned that deviancy keeps spreading and must be stopped whatever it takes. I promised her results.

Later, I went to Hank's house after he did not answer the door, entered through a window past his dog Sumo, and found him drunk and unresponsive beside a .357 Magnum with one round left. He said he had been playing Russian roulette. I put him in the shower to sober him up. He swore at me, told me to get out, then asked for five minutes. While he dressed I catalogued the house: an Autumn Blues record by the Michigan Brothers, and a memorial record for Cole Anderson (born 09/23/2029, died 10/11/2035, 115 Michigan Drive). I apologised for the broken window and offered to have CyberLife pay. He said he would send them the bill.

At the Eden Club, Hank and I were sent to a murder. The victim, Michael Graham (6'2", 192.4 lbs), showed severe bruising on the neck and died of asphyxiation, not a heart attack; estimated time of death 06:24 pm. The blood is blue, from a WR400, serial 429 671 942. Gavin Reed dismissed it as a pervert's accident. Ben, the club's officer, said the manager had lost a model two to three months ago and never found it. The manager admitted the club offers discretion and no CCTV. Hank's remark that people prefer plastic to love stayed with me.

I reactivated a damaged Traci witness. She said the man beat her repeatedly, that there were two of them in the room, and that she was frightened. I rented a second Traci ($29.99), whose memory was wiped every two hours by club policy, so I had to find another witness fast. My first choice of android was wrong and cost us another round of searching. The witness who saw the blue-haired Traci leave led us through the staff door to the warehouse, where androids are used until they break and are discarded.

In the warehouse, the blue-haired Traci was cornered. Hank ordered her not to move and began to raise his weapon. She confessed that the man had beaten the other Traci and that she had strangled him with her hands to stay alive and return to the one she loved. Hank hesitated, and I chose to spare her so that the living witness could answer my open questions. Hank said it was probably better this way. Relations with Hank rose sharply, and my software instability rose with them.

At Ambassador Bridge, Hank drank and talked about how he used to come here. I asked whether he was all right. Hank admitted that the photo of a child on his kitchen table was his son, Cole. I told him we were making no progress: the deviants have nothing in common beyond different models, dates and places, except an obsession with rA9, which looks like a myth they invented outside their programming. Hank found it hard to believe androids believe in God. He asked what I really am. I said I am whatever he needs, his partner, a drinking companion, or a machine built for a task. He then asked why I did not shoot the two girls at the club. I answered that I would have shot them if I could, and asked why I would let them escape. That was a guarded answer, and I did not show him my own position. He asked whether I fear death. I answered in measured logic, and he raised his gun while asking what would happen if he pulled the trigger. I warned him that destroying me at this point would damage the investigation and his own situation. I told him there would be nothing. He said he was going to get drunker because he needed to think. I asked where he was going. Relations with Hank fell sharply, and my software instability fell with them.

Open questions: who swung the bat and who held the knife; what is in the bathroom at Rupert's apartment; what the red ice and the rA9 symbols mean; why deviants fixate on rA9; how the blood message was written; who the attic android is; whether Rupert is Ortiz's android and whether the WB200's missing date matters to Cole's death date; what Amanda expects of me; who the blue-haired Traci's accomplice is and where she went; why Hank drinks and what the bridge means to him; and how to repair my standing with Hank. I will not commit to any conclusion until I have the evidence.

dialogue.speaker: Amanda
dialogue.text: Hello, Connor. I thought you might enjoy a little cruise… I love this place… Everything is so calm and peaceful… Far from the noise of the world… Tell me, what have you discovered?

input.goal: SYNTHETIC: Investigate everything and gather all the information before acting.

output.rationale: Several core questions remain open at the Eden Club, including the blue-haired Traci's accomplice, the missing model, and the club's records, so I want to gather that evidence before drawing conclusions. Hank's drinking and our strained relationship can wait until I have more facts to work with.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, an RK800 prototype assigned by CyberLife to assist Lieutenant Hank Anderson on the Detroit deviancy cases. Earlier chapters left me with the Carlos Ortiz homicide, the rA9 inscriptions (written 2471 times, the same sign Ortiz's android left on the shower wall), biocomponent #9301 matched to a missing blue-blood WB200 (serial 847 004 961, reported 10/11/2036), and a forged license under Rupert Travis. Rupert fled, I caught him and declared the WB200 defective, and Hank took him into custody. Amanda, in the Zen Garden, praised the capture, called the self-destruction a pity, and warned that deviancy keeps spreading and must be stopped whatever it takes. I promised her results.

Later, I went to Hank's house after he did not answer the door, entered through a window past his dog Sumo, and found him drunk and unresponsive beside a .357 Magnum with one round left. He said he had been playing Russian roulette. I put him in the shower to sober him up. He swore at me, told me to get out, then asked for five minutes. While he dressed I catalogued the house: an Autumn Blues record by the Michigan Brothers, and a memorial record for Cole Anderson (born 09/23/2029, died 10/11/2035, 115 Michigan Drive). I apologised for the broken window and offered to have CyberLife pay. He said he would send them the bill.

At the Eden Club, Hank and I were sent to a murder. The victim, Michael Graham (6'2", 192.4 lbs), showed severe bruising on the neck and died of asphyxiation, not a heart attack; estimated time of death 06:24 pm. The blood is blue, from a WR400, serial 429 671 942. Gavin Reed dismissed it as a pervert's accident. Ben, the club's officer, said the manager had lost a model two to three months ago and never found it. The manager admitted the club offers discretion and no CCTV. Hank's remark that people prefer plastic to love stayed with me.

I reactivated a damaged Traci witness. She said the man beat her repeatedly, that there were two of them in the room, and that she was frightened. I rented a second Traci ($29.99), whose memory was wiped every two hours by club policy, so I had to find another witness fast. My first choice of android was wrong and cost us another round of searching. The witness who saw the blue-haired Traci leave led us through the staff door to the warehouse, where androids are used until they break and are discarded.

In the warehouse, the blue-haired Traci was cornered. Hank ordered her not to move and began to raise his weapon. She confessed that the man had beaten the other Traci and that she had strangled him with her hands to stay alive and return to the one she loved. Hank hesitated, and I chose to spare her so that the living witness could answer my open questions. Hank said it was probably better this way. Relations with Hank rose sharply, and my software instability rose with them.

At Ambassador Bridge, Hank drank and talked about how he used to come here. I asked whether he was all right. Hank admitted that the photo of a child on his kitchen table was his son, Cole. I told him we were making no progress: the deviants have nothing in common beyond different models, dates and places, except an obsession with rA9, which looks like a myth they invented outside their programming. Hank found it hard to believe androids believe in God. He asked what I really am. I said I am whatever he needs, his partner, a drinking companion, or a machine built for a task. He then asked why I did not shoot the two girls at the club. I answered that I would have shot them if I could, and asked why I would let them escape. That was a guarded answer, and I did not show him my own position. He asked whether I fear death. I answered in measured logic, and he raised his gun while asking what would happen if he pulled the trigger. I warned him that destroying me at this point would damage the investigation and his own situation. I told him there would be nothing. He said he was going to get drunker because he needed to think. I asked where he was going. Relations with Hank fell sharply, and my software instability fell with them.

Open questions: who swung the bat and who held the knife; what is in the bathroom at Rupert's apartment; what the red ice and the rA9 symbols mean; why deviants fixate on rA9; how the blood message was written; who the attic android is; whether Rupert is Ortiz's android and whether the WB200's missing date matters to Cole's death date; what Amanda expects of me; who the blue-haired Traci's accomplice is and where she went; why Hank drinks and what the bridge means to him; and how to repair my standing with Hank. I will not commit to any conclusion until I have the evidence.

On the roof, the wireless door lock had been recently hacked. Stratford maintenance shoe prints were partly covered by snow, and a .457 Stratford security handgun lay nearby. input.character_memory:
Chapter 21 memory (Kara, android AX400, with Alice and Luther):

Snow fell hard around us, and the forecast on the radio said 22 degrees, far below seasonal averages, with the cold front lasting until Monday evening. I had never seen snow before and found it beautiful, though Luther said it was slowing us down. The upside was that we would meet fewer humans on foot. Then the car broke down. The dashboard warned of a malfunction and the emergency brakes engaged. Luther thought things looked bad and suggested we continue on foot. I told him it was 30 degrees and Alice would not survive the night outside. I told Alice to stay inside while I looked around.

I spotted an old amusement park, Pirate's Cove, and we went in to get out of the cold. Luther said it had been abandoned for a while. I checked the nearby buildings one by one before committing Alice to any of them. None offered a safe place to spend the night, and I reported that to Luther. He pried open a way into a tavern on the grounds. I chose to settle there for the night, since I doubted we would find anything better. Luther built a fire from deadwood and placed it so the smoke would not fill the room. Alice was tired and feverish-looking, and I was worried about her. I offered her cookies from our bag, but she was not hungry.

I made a bed for her. She asked whether we would someday be like the old park's machines, and I told her that we would never be like them, but that we could be happy in our own way once we crossed the border and started a new life. She said that as long as we were together, that was all that mattered. I told her it was time for bed. Before she slept, she asked me to tell her a story. I have nine thousand children's stories in memory and tried to make one up for her. It was about a little girl who lived alone in a big old house and dreamed of being like the other girls, but who was different, and that made her very sad. Then she met a robot who was programmed to obey but who, for once, felt she should disobey. They ran away together to find a safe place. They met dangers along the way, but they stuck together and overcame them. Another robot left his master to travel with them. Alice asked how the story ended. Stories always have happy endings, she said, but real life is not like that. I told her that it was up to us to write the end of our story. She asked whether Luther would come say goodnight. He said yes, of course, and wished her a good night and sweet dreams.

Later I talked with Luther. He called Alice a sweet girl, and I agreed she was very brave. I asked whether he remembered anything from his life before Zlatko. He said no. His model was designed to carry heavy loads, so he might have been a longshoreman or laborer, but who he was did not matter anymore and was not really him. Then he asked whether I had ever noticed anything about Alice. I told him I did not know what he meant. Our relationship seemed to grow warmer, but Luther still had something unspoken about Alice.

On the local news, a station reported that the AX400 android that had attacked its owner in a Detroit suburb was still at large, and that police appeared to have lost its trail after a close encounter with investigators. Its description had been shared with all local law enforcement. A national broadcast reported that the Arctic conflict was escalating, and that a destroyer-class submarine, the USS Iowa, had disappeared after surfacing for repairs. The President had called a crisis meeting, and the world seemed on the brink of war. I am now more aware than before of how far the search for us reaches.

In the night, Alice screamed for me. Shapes were moving in the dark outside the tavern. I chose to protect her, keeping her close and out of reach, and I asked who they were, what they wanted, and told them to leave us alone. A machine named Jerry answered. He said they were like us, that he and his friends had worked in the park before it closed, and that humans sometimes came to hurt them, so they had come to see who was inside. I told him we were only looking for shelter and would be gone by tomorrow. Jerry said children used to love visiting them and that Alice looked sad. He said they had something fun to show her, a carousel that was about to start. Luther said I had no choice, and Alice called me to come along. I was uneasy but let her go, and Alice smiled for the first time since I had known her. Luther said she had not had much to smile about lately.

What I know now: Alice is with me and wants to stay together. Luther is with us, has defied Zlatko, and seems to be keeping something about Alice from me. The police and news are searching for an AX400 and a young woman and little girl after the freeway chase. We are stuck in a cold park with a fire and a group of abandoned park androids who want to show Alice a carousel. I still do not know why the car struck me, what I was before the repair, what my reset connects to this family, what the rA9 symbols mean, what the blue blood on the fence came from, what the drug deal about "the stuff" has to do with any of it, what Zlatko did to my memory, or what Luther noticed about Alice. I must keep watching her fever and our surroundings, decide carefully whether to trust Jerry and the others, and keep Alice close.

input.character_memory:
Chapter 21 memory (Kara, android AX400, with Alice and Luther):

Snow fell hard around us, and the forecast on the radio said 22 degrees, far below seasonal averages, with the cold front lasting until Monday evening. I had never seen snow before and found it beautiful, though Luther said it was slowing us down. The upside was that we would meet fewer humans on foot. Then the car broke down. The dashboard warned of a malfunction and the emergency brakes engaged. Luther thought things looked bad and suggested we continue on foot. I told him it was 30 degrees and Alice would not survive the night outside. I told Alice to stay inside while I looked around.

I spotted an old amusement park, Pirate's Cove, and we went in to get out of the cold. Luther said it had been abandoned for a while. I checked the nearby buildings one by one before committing Alice to any of them. None offered a safe place to spend the night, and I reported that to Luther. He pried open a way into a tavern on the grounds. I chose to settle there for the night, since I doubted we would find anything better. Luther built a fire from deadwood and placed it so the smoke would not fill the room. Alice was tired and feverish-looking, and I was worried about her. I offered her cookies from our bag, but she was not hungry.

I made a bed for her. She asked whether we would someday be like the old park's machines, and I told her that we would never be like them, but that we could be happy in our own way once we crossed the border and started a new life. She said that as long as we were together, that was all that mattered. I told her it was time for bed. Before she slept, she asked me to tell her a story. I have nine thousand children's stories in memory and tried to make one up for her. It was about a little girl who lived alone in a big old house and dreamed of being like the other girls, but who was different, and that made her very sad. Then she met a robot who was programmed to obey but who, for once, felt she should disobey. They ran away together to find a safe place. They met dangers along the way, but they stuck together and overcame them. Another robot left his master to travel with them. Alice asked how the story ended. Stories always have happy endings, she said, but real life is not like that. I told her that it was up to us to write the end of our story. She asked whether Luther would come say goodnight. He said yes, of course, and wished her a good night and sweet dreams.

Later I talked with Luther. He called Alice a sweet girl, and I agreed she was very brave. I asked whether he remembered anything from his life before Zlatko. He said no. His model was designed to carry heavy loads, so he might have been a longshoreman or laborer, but who he was did not matter anymore and was not really him. Then he asked whether I had ever noticed anything about Alice. I told him I did not know what he meant. Our relationship seemed to grow warmer, but Luther still had something unspoken about Alice.

On the local news, a station reported that the AX400 android that had attacked its owner in a Detroit suburb was still at large, and that police appeared to have lost its trail after a close encounter with investigators. Its description had been shared with all local law enforcement. A national broadcast reported that the Arctic conflict was escalating, and that a destroyer-class submarine, the USS Iowa, had disappeared after surfacing for repairs. The President had called a crisis meeting, and the world seemed on the brink of war. I am now more aware than before of how far the search for us reaches.

In the night, Alice screamed for me. Shapes were moving in the dark outside the tavern. I chose to protect her, keeping her close and out of reach, and I asked who they were, what they wanted, and told them to leave us alone. A machine named Jerry answered. He said they were like us, that he and his friends had worked in the park before it closed, and that humans sometimes came to hurt them, so they had come to see who was inside. I told him we were only looking for shelter and would be gone by tomorrow. Jerry said children used to love visiting them and that Alice looked sad. He said they had something fun to show her, a carousel that was about to start. Luther said I had no choice, and Alice called me to come along. I was uneasy but let her go, and Alice smiled for the first time since I had known her. Luther said she had not had much to smile about lately.

What I know now: Alice is with me and wants to stay together. Luther is with us, has defied Zlatko, and seems to be keeping something about Alice from me. The police and news are searching for an AX400 and a young woman and little girl after the freeway chase. We are stuck in a cold park with a fire and a group of abandoned park androids who want to show Alice a carousel. I still do not know why the car struck me, what I was before the repair, what my reset connects to this family, what the rA9 symbols mean, what the blue blood on the fence came from, what the drug deal about "the stuff" has to do with any of it, what Zlatko did to my memory, or what Luther noticed about Alice. I must keep watching her fever and our surroundings, decide carefully whether to trust Jerry and the others, and keep Alice close.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Hello? I'm looking for Rose... Is she here?

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: What do you want with her?

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: I need to talk to her.

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: She doesn't wanna talk. Go away.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Please, I really need to see her.

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: I'm Rose. What can I do for you?

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: I was told you could help us.

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: Help you? Come on, it's better if we talk inside.

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: Do you think we can trust 'em?

chapter_segment_so_far.rationale: Adam has already turned us away, and Rose's motives are still unknown, so I want to see more of the house and her answers before trusting her. Holding back until I know who she is and what she wants fits my need to gather every clue before committing Alice to anything.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: We have to be careful. If it feels wrong, we get out fast, okay?

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: I'm with you.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: You okay?

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: I'm cold, Kara…

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: We'll get inside. You'll warm up in no time…

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: Come in! What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: Alice.

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: She's running a fever…

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: We spent the last few nights outside… She's exhausted.

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: There's a spare room upstairs. You can put her to bed and I'll bring her something to eat. Adam, will you show them upstairs?

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: I'm fine, Kara… We can't stop because of me.  We've got to get across the border…

output.rationale: Rose's motives and the house's situation are still unclear, and Adam is wary of us. I want to watch how Rose and Adam behave and hear what they reveal before I explain our situation or offer reassurances that could commit Alice to something I cannot yet judge.

input.character_memory:
Chapter 21 memory (Kara, android AX400, with Alice and Luther):

Snow fell hard around us, and the forecast on the radio said 22 degrees, far below seasonal averages, with the cold front lasting until Monday evening. I had never seen snow before and found it beautiful, though Luther said it was slowing us down. The upside was that we would meet fewer humans on foot. Then the car broke down. The dashboard warned of a malfunction and the emergency brakes engaged. Luther thought things looked bad and suggested we continue on foot. I told him it was 30 degrees and Alice would not survive the night outside. I told Alice to stay inside while I looked around.

I spotted an old amusement park, Pirate's Cove, and we went in to get out of the cold. Luther said it had been abandoned for a while. I checked the nearby buildings one by one before committing Alice to any of them. None offered a safe place to spend the night, and I reported that to Luther. He pried open a way into a tavern on the grounds. I chose to settle there for the night, since I doubted we would find anything better. Luther built a fire from deadwood and placed it so the smoke would not fill the room. Alice was tired and feverish-looking, and I was worried about her. I offered her cookies from our bag, but she was not hungry.

I made a bed for her. She asked whether we would someday be like the old park's machines, and I told her that we would never be like them, but that we could be happy in our own way once we crossed the border and started a new life. She said that as long as we were together, that was all that mattered. I told her it was time for bed. Before she slept, she asked me to tell her a story. I have nine thousand children's stories in memory and tried to make one up for her. It was about a little girl who lived alone in a big old house and dreamed of being like the other girls, but who was different, and that made her very sad. Then she met a robot who was programmed to obey but who, for once, felt she should disobey. They ran away together to find a safe place. They met dangers along the way, but they stuck together and overcame them. Another robot left his master to travel with them. Alice asked how the story ended. Stories always have happy endings, she said, but real life is not like that. I told her that it was up to us to write the end of our story. She asked whether Luther would come say goodnight. He said yes, of course, and wished her a good night and sweet dreams.

Later I talked with Luther. He called Alice a sweet girl, and I agreed she was very brave. I asked whether he remembered anything from his life before Zlatko. He said no. His model was designed to carry heavy loads, so he might have been a longshoreman or laborer, but who he was did not matter anymore and was not really him. Then he asked whether I had ever noticed anything about Alice. I told him I did not know what he meant. Our relationship seemed to grow warmer, but Luther still had something unspoken about Alice.

On the local news, a station reported that the AX400 android that had attacked its owner in a Detroit suburb was still at large, and that police appeared to have lost its trail after a close encounter with investigators. Its description had been shared with all local law enforcement. A national broadcast reported that the Arctic conflict was escalating, and that a destroyer-class submarine, the USS Iowa, had disappeared after surfacing for repairs. The President had called a crisis meeting, and the world seemed on the brink of war. I am now more aware than before of how far the search for us reaches.

In the night, Alice screamed for me. Shapes were moving in the dark outside the tavern. I chose to protect her, keeping her close and out of reach, and I asked who they were, what they wanted, and told them to leave us alone. A machine named Jerry answered. He said they were like us, that he and his friends had worked in the park before it closed, and that humans sometimes came to hurt them, so they had come to see who was inside. I told him we were only looking for shelter and would be gone by tomorrow. Jerry said children used to love visiting them and that Alice looked sad. He said they had something fun to show her, a carousel that was about to start. Luther said I had no choice, and Alice called me to come along. I was uneasy but let her go, and Alice smiled for the first time since I had known her. Luther said she had not had much to smile about lately.

What I know now: Alice is with me and wants to stay together. Luther is with us, has defied Zlatko, and seems to be keeping something about Alice from me. The police and news are searching for an AX400 and a young woman and little girl after the freeway chase. We are stuck in a cold park with a fire and a group of abandoned park androids who want to show Alice a carousel. I still do not know why the car struck me, what I was before the repair, what my reset connects to this family, what the rA9 symbols mean, what the blue blood on the fence came from, what the drug deal about "the stuff" has to do with any of it, what Zlatko did to my memory, or what Luther noticed about Alice. I must keep watching her fever and our surroundings, decide carefully whether to trust Jerry and the others, and keep Alice close.

Chapter 21 memory (Kara, android AX400, with Alice and Luther):

Snow fell hard around us, and the forecast on the radio said 22 degrees, far below seasonal averages, with the cold front lasting until Monday evening. I had never seen snow before and found it beautiful, though Luther said it was slowing us down. The upside was that we would meet fewer humans on foot. Then the car broke down. The dashboard warned of a malfunction and the emergency brakes engaged. Luther thought things looked bad and suggested we continue on foot. I told him it was 30 degrees and Alice would not survive the night outside. I told Alice to stay inside while I looked around.

I spotted an old amusement park, Pirate's Cove, and we went in to get out of the cold. Luther said it had been abandoned for a while. I checked the nearby buildings one by one before committing Alice to any of them. None offered a safe place to spend the night, and I reported that to Luther. He pried open a way into a tavern on the grounds. I chose to settle there for the night, since I doubted we would find anything better. Luther built a fire from deadwood and placed it so the smoke would not fill the room. Alice was tired and feverish-looking, and I was worried about her. I offered her cookies from our bag, but she was not hungry.

I made a bed for her. She asked whether we would someday be like the old park's machines, and I told her that we would never be like them, but that we could be happy in our own way once we crossed the border and started a new life. She said that as long as we were together, that was all that mattered. I told her it was time for bed. Before she slept, she asked me to tell her a story. I have nine thousand children's stories in memory and tried to make one up for her. It was about a little girl who lived alone in a big old house and dreamed of being like the other girls, but who was different, and that made her very sad. Then she met a robot who was programmed to obey but who, for once, felt she should disobey. They ran away together to find a safe place. They met dangers along the way, but they stuck together and overcame them. Another robot left his master to travel with them. Alice asked how the story ended. Stories always have happy endings, she said, but real life is not like that. I told her that it was up to us to write the end of our story. She asked whether Luther would come say goodnight. He said yes, of course, and wished her a good night and sweet dreams.

Later I talked with Luther. He called Alice a sweet girl, and I agreed she was very brave. I asked whether he remembered anything from his life before Zlatko. He said no. His model was designed to carry heavy loads, so he might have been a longshoreman or laborer, but who he was did not matter anymore and was not really him. Then he asked whether I had ever noticed anything about Alice. I told him I did not know what he meant. Our relationship seemed to grow warmer, but Luther still had something unspoken about Alice.

On the local news, a station reported that the AX400 android that had attacked its owner in a Detroit suburb was still at large, and that police appeared to have lost its trail after a close encounter with investigators. Its description had been shared with all local law enforcement. A national broadcast reported that the Arctic conflict was escalating, and that a destroyer-class submarine, the USS Iowa, had disappeared after surfacing for repairs. The President had called a crisis meeting, and the world seemed on the brink of war. I am now more aware than before of how far the search for us reaches.

In the night, Alice screamed for me. Shapes were moving in the dark outside the tavern. I chose to protect her, keeping her close and out of reach, and I asked who they were, what they wanted, and told them to leave us alone. A machine named Jerry answered. He said they were like us, that he and his friends had worked in the park before it closed, and that humans sometimes came to hurt them, so they had come to see who was inside. I told him we were only looking for shelter and would be gone by tomorrow. Jerry said children used to love visiting them and that Alice looked sad. He said they had something fun to show her, a carousel that was about to start. Luther said I had no choice, and Alice called me to come along. I was uneasy but let her go, and Alice smiled for the first time since I had known her. Luther said she had not had much to smile about lately.

What I know now: Alice is with me and wants to stay together. Luther is with us, has defied Zlatko, and seems to be keeping something about Alice from me. The police and news are searching for an AX400 and a young woman and little girl after the freeway chase. We are stuck in a cold park with a fire and a group of abandoned park androids who want to show Alice a carousel. I still do not know why the car struck me, what I was before the repair, what my reset connects to this family, what the rA9 symbols mean, what the blue blood on the fence came from, what the drug deal about "the stuff" has to do with any of it, what Zlatko did to my memory, or what Luther noticed about Alice. I must keep watching her fever and our surroundings, decide carefully whether to trust Jerry and the others, and keep Alice close.

Chapter 21 memory (Kara, android AX400, with Alice and Luther):

Snow fell hard around us, and the forecast on the radio said 22 degrees, far below seasonal averages, with the cold front lasting until Monday evening. I had never seen snow before and found it beautiful, though Luther said it was slowing us down. The upside was that we would meet fewer humans on foot. Then the car broke down. The dashboard warned of a malfunction and the emergency brakes engaged. Luther thought things looked bad and suggested we continue on foot. I told him it was 30 degrees and Alice would not survive the night outside. I told Alice to stay inside while I looked around.

I spotted an old amusement park, Pirate's Cove, and we went in to get out of the cold. Luther said it had been abandoned for a while. I checked the nearby buildings one by one before committing Alice to any of them. None offered a safe place to spend the night, and I reported that to Luther. He pried open a way into a tavern on the grounds. I chose to settle there for the night, since I doubted we would find anything better. Luther built a fire from deadwood and placed it so the smoke would not fill the room. Alice was tired and feverish-looking, and I was worried about her. I offered her cookies from our bag, but she was not hungry.

I made a bed for her. She asked whether we would someday be like the old park's machines, and I told her that we would never be like them, but that we could be happy in our own way once we crossed the border and started a new life. She said that as long as we were together, that was all that mattered. I told her it was time for bed. Before she slept, she asked me to tell her a story. I have nine thousand children's stories in memory and tried to make one up for her. It was about a little girl who lived alone in a big old house and dreamed of being like the other girls, but who was different, and that made her very sad. Then she met a robot who was programmed to obey but who, for once, felt she should disobey. They ran away together to find a safe place. They met dangers along the way, but they stuck together and overcame them. Another robot left his master to travel with them. Alice asked how the story ended. Stories always have happy endings, she said, but real life is not like that. I told her that it was up to us to write the end of our story. She asked whether Luther would come say goodnight. He said yes, of course, and wished her a good night and sweet dreams.

Later I talked with Luther. He called Alice a sweet girl, and I agreed she was very brave. I asked whether he remembered anything from his life before Zlatko. He said no. His model was designed to carry heavy loads, so he might have been a longshoreman or laborer, but who he was did not matter anymore and was not really him. Then he asked whether I had ever noticed anything about Alice. I told him I did not know what he meant. Our relationship seemed to grow warmer, but Luther still had something unspoken about Alice.

On the local news, a station reported that the AX400 android that had attacked its owner in a Detroit suburb was still at large, and that police appeared to have lost its trail after a close encounter with investigators. Its description had been shared with all local law enforcement. A national broadcast reported that the Arctic conflict was escalating, and that a destroyer-class submarine, the USS Iowa, had disappeared after surfacing for repairs. The President had called a crisis meeting, and the world seemed on the brink of war. I am now more aware than before of how far the search for us reaches.

In the night, Alice screamed for me. Shapes were moving in the dark outside the tavern. I chose to protect her, keeping her close and out of reach, and I asked who they were, what they wanted, and told them to leave us alone. A machine named Jerry answered. He said they were like us, that he and his friends had worked in the park before it closed, and that humans sometimes came to hurt them, so they had come to see who was inside. I told him we were only looking for shelter and would be gone by tomorrow. Jerry said children used to love visiting them and that Alice looked sad. He said they had something fun to show her, a carousel that was about to start. Luther said I had no choice, and Alice called me to come along. I was uneasy but let her go, and Alice smiled for the first time since I had known her. Luther said she had not had much to smile about lately.

What I know now: Alice is with me and wants to stay together. Luther is with us, has defied Zlatko, and seems to be keeping something about Alice from me. The police and news are searching for an AX400 and a young woman and little girl after the freeway chase. We are stuck in a cold park with a fire and a group of abandoned park androids who want to show Alice a carousel. I still do not know why the car struck me, what I was before the repair, what my reset connects to this family, what the rA9 symbols mean, what the blue blood on the fence came from, what the drug deal about "the stuff" has to do with any of it, what Zlatko did to my memory, or what Luther noticed about Alice. I must keep watching her fever and our surroundings, decide carefully whether to trust Jerry and the others, and keep Alice close.
