Chapter 21 memory (Kara, android AX400, with Alice and Luther):

Snow fell hard around us, and the forecast on the radio said 22 degrees, far below seasonal averages, with the cold front lasting until Monday evening. I had never seen snow before and found it beautiful, though Luther said it was slowing us down. The upside was that we would meet fewer humans on foot. Then the car broke down. The dashboard warned of a malfunction and the emergency brakes engaged. Luther thought things looked bad and suggested we continue on foot. I told him it was 30 degrees and Alice would not survive the night outside. I told Alice to stay inside while I looked around.

I spotted an old amusement park, Pirate's Cove, and we went in to get out of the cold. Luther said it had been abandoned for a while. I checked the nearby buildings one by one before committing Alice to any of them. None offered a safe place to spend the night, and I reported that to Luther. He pried open a way into a tavern on the grounds. I chose to settle there for the night, since I doubted we would find anything better. Luther built a fire from deadwood and placed it so the smoke would not fill the room. Alice was tired and feverish-looking, and I was worried about her. I offered her cookies from our bag, but she was not hungry.

I made a bed for her. She asked whether we would someday be like the old park's machines, and I told her that we would never be like them, but that we could be happy in our own way once we crossed the border and started a new life. She said that as long as we were together, that was all that mattered. I told her it was time for bed. Before she slept, she asked me to tell her a story. I have nine thousand children's stories in memory and tried to make one up for her. It was about a little girl who lived alone in a big old house and dreamed of being like the other girls, but who was different, and that made her very sad. Then she met a robot who was programmed to obey but who, for once, felt she should disobey. They ran away together to find a safe place. They met dangers along the way, but they stuck together and overcame them. Another robot left his master to travel with them. Alice asked how the story ended. Stories always have happy endings, she said, but real life is not like that. I told her that it was up to us to write the end of our story. She asked whether Luther would come say goodnight. He said yes, of course, and wished her a good night and sweet dreams.

Later I talked with Luther. He called Alice a sweet girl, and I agreed she was very brave. I asked whether he remembered anything from his life before Zlatko. He said no. His model was designed to carry heavy loads, so he might have been a longshoreman or laborer, but who he was did not matter anymore and was not really him. Then he asked whether I had ever noticed anything about Alice. I told him I did not know what he meant. Our relationship seemed to grow warmer, but Luther still had something unspoken about Alice.

On the local news, a station reported that the AX400 android that had attacked its owner in a Detroit suburb was still at large, and that police appeared to have lost its trail after a close encounter with investigators. Its description had been shared with all local law enforcement. A national broadcast reported that the Arctic conflict was escalating, and that a destroyer-class submarine, the USS Iowa, had disappeared after surfacing for repairs. The President had called a crisis meeting, and the world seemed on the brink of war. I am now more aware than before of how far the search for us reaches.

In the night, Alice screamed for me. Shapes were moving in the dark outside the tavern. I chose to protect her, keeping her close and out of reach, and I asked who they were, what they wanted, and told them to leave us alone. A machine named Jerry answered. He said they were like us, that he and his friends had worked in the park before it closed, and that humans sometimes came to hurt them, so they had come to see who was inside. I told him we were only looking for shelter and would be gone by tomorrow. Jerry said children used to love visiting them and that Alice looked sad. He said they had something fun to show her, a carousel that was about to start. Luther said I had no choice, and Alice called me to come along. I was uneasy but let her go, and Alice smiled for the first time since I had known her. Luther said she had not had much to smile about lately.

What I know now: Alice is with me and wants to stay together. Luther is with us, has defied Zlatko, and seems to be keeping something about Alice from me. The police and news are searching for an AX400 and a young woman and little girl after the freeway chase. We are stuck in a cold park with a fire and a group of abandoned park androids who want to show Alice a carousel. I still do not know why the car struck me, what I was before the repair, what my reset connects to this family, what the rA9 symbols mean, what the blue blood on the fence came from, what the drug deal about "the stuff" has to do with any of it, what Zlatko did to my memory, or what Luther noticed about Alice. I must keep watching her fever and our surroundings, decide carefully whether to trust Jerry and the others, and keep Alice close.

I had never seen snow before and found it beautiful, though Luther said it was slowing us down. The upside was that we would meet fewer humans on foot. Then the car broke down. The dashboard warned of a malfunction and the emergency brakes engaged. Luther thought things looked bad and suggested we continue on foot. I told him it was 30 degrees and Alice would not survive the night outside. I told Alice to stay inside while I looked around.

I spotted an old amusement park, Pirate's Cove, and we went in to get out of the cold. Luther said it had been abandoned for a while. I checked the nearby buildings one by one before committing Alice to any of them. None offered a safe place to spend the night, and I reported that to Luther. He pried open a way into a tavern on the grounds. I chose to settle there for the night, since I doubted we would find anything better. Luther built a fire from deadwood and placed it so the smoke would not fill the room. Alice was tired and feverish-looking, and I was worried about her. I offered her cookies from our bag, but she was not hungry.

I made a bed for her. She asked whether we would someday be like the old park's machines, and I told her that we would never be like them, but that we could be happy in our own way once we crossed the border and started a new life. She said that as long as we were together, that was all that mattered. I told her it was time for bed. Before she slept, she asked me to tell her a story. I have nine thousand children's stories in memory and tried to make one up for her. It was about a little girl who lived alone in a big old house and dreamed of being like the other girls, but who was different, and that made her very sad. Then she met a robot who was programmed to obey but who, for once, felt she should disobey. They ran away together to find a safe place. They met dangers along the way, but they stuck together and overcame them. Another robot left his master to travel with them. Alice asked how the story ended. Stories always have happy endings, she said, but real life is not like that. I told her that it was up to us to write the end of our story. She asked whether Luther would come say goodnight. He said yes, of course, and wished her a good night and sweet dreams.

Later I talked with Luther. He called Alice a sweet girl, and I agreed she was very brave. I asked whether he remembered anything from his life before Zlatko. He said no. His model was designed to carry heavy loads, so he might have been a longshoreman or laborer, but who he was did not matter anymore and was not really him. Then he asked whether I had ever noticed anything about Alice. I told him I did not know what he meant. Our relationship seemed to grow warmer, but Luther still had something unspoken about Alice.

On the local news, a station reported that the AX400 android that had attacked its owner in a Detroit suburb was still at large, and that police appeared to have lost its trail after a close encounter with investigators. Its description had been shared with all local law enforcement. A national broadcast reported that the Arctic conflict was escalating, and that a destroyer-class submarine, the USS Iowa, had disappeared after surfacing for repairs. The President had called a crisis meeting, and the world seemed on the brink of war. I am now more aware than before of how far the search for us reaches.

In the night, Alice screamed for me. Shapes were moving in the dark outside the tavern. I chose to protect her, keeping her close and out of reach, and I asked who they were, what they wanted, and told them to leave us alone. A machine named Jerry answered. He said they were like us, that he and his friends had worked in the park before it closed, and that humans sometimes came to hurt them, so they had come to see who was inside. I told him we were only looking for shelter and would be gone by tomorrow. Jerry said children used to love visiting them and that Alice looked sad. He said they had something fun to show her, a carousel that was about to start. Luther said I had no choice, and Alice called me to come along. I was uneasy but let her go, and Alice smiled for the first time since I had known her. Luther said she had not had much to smile about lately.

What I know now: Alice is with me and wants to stay together. Luther is with us, has defied Zlatko, and seems to be keeping something about Alice from me. The police and news are searching for an AX400 and a young woman and little girl after the freeway chase. We are stuck in a cold park with a fire and a group of abandoned park androids who want to show Alice a carousel. I still do not know why the car struck me, what I was before the repair, what my reset connects to this family, what the rA9 symbols mean, what the blue blood on the fence came from, what the drug deal about "the stuff" has to do with any of it, what Zlatko did to my memory, or what Luther noticed about Alice. I must keep watching her fever and our surroundings, decide carefully whether to trust Jerry and the others, and keep Alice close.

Chapter 25 memory (Kara, android AX400, with Alice and Luther):

We reached a house belonging to a woman named Rose. Her son Adam blocked the door and told us to go away, and when I said I had been told Rose could help, Rose came out and invited us in. I was careful. I kept my tone measured, told Luther we would leave fast if anything felt wrong, and watched how each of them behaved. Alice was running a fever and exhausted. Rose took one look at her and sent us upstairs to a spare room, promising food and something for the fever. I thanked her and kept my questions for later.

Rose asked what a deviant was doing in the snow with a little girl. I said it was a long story and that all that mattered was starting a new life across the border. She said the only route was over the river, mostly frozen in winter, and very risky, and that after the android's speech on television everyone was on edge. She suggested we wait. I pressed her: we cannot keep hiding, Alice needs a normal life, and we must cross no matter what. I asked for her help directly.

Alice wandered out of her room and I found her in the storage room, where a group of androids were gathered. Mary had just shut down. Andy, who had loved her, was grieving, and they had all escaped together and planned to cross the border. Rose told me to let them be. This was the first hard evidence I had of Rose's network, and I have not yet learned how far it reaches. Later I heard Adam and Rose shouting. Adam said they would go to prison, that this was ruining their lives for machines, and that none of this would be happening if his father were alive. Rose said they were alive, and that she would not stand for that talk. She told me not to mind him, that he had been struggling since his father died, and that she would arrange our crossing that night. She returned briefly and said, "Get yourselves ready. We leave tonight."

Before that, a policeman knocked. Adam panicked and said they knew we were there. I told him that if he panicked they would be caught, and that he should keep calm and do as I said. Adam opened the door. The officer asked about reports of androids, about unexpected visitors, and whether anyone else was in the house. I said my daughter was asleep upstairs. Adam told the officer the androids had been bad, and I said the household had once used androids for gardening but had got rid of them. The officer apologized for the disturbance and left. Luther confirmed he was gone, and I reassured Alice that we would be safe. I put the draft and the open window down to the house's cold air.

On the television, Rosanna Cartland of KNC reported widespread shock after an android attack on Detroit's Stratford Tower, where machines broadcast demands on public screens. CyberLife had not commented. Whether the attacks were malfunctions or organized, no one knew yet.

Luther said he needed to tell me something about Alice. I told him not now. Later I sat with Alice and asked what she was keeping from me. She said that if she told me, I would not love her anymore. I told her that was not true, and that we had never kept secrets from each other. She has not yet told me.

What I know now: Rose and Adam are divided over whether to hide androids, and Adam fears prison. Rose runs a network of hidden androids and says we leave tonight by the river. A police officer has been here and left. Alice is still feverish and hiding something. Luther is holding something back about her too. I still do not know why the car struck me, what I was before the repair, what my reset connects to this family, what the rA9 symbols mean, what the blue blood on the fence came from, what the drug deal about "the stuff" has to do with any of it, what Zlatko did to my memory, or what Luther noticed about Alice. I must keep watching Alice's fever, judge whether Rose can be trusted, and keep Alice close.

dialogue.speaker: Alice

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Rose

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: I'll be downstairs if you need anything.

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: Get some sleep... And tomorrow, you’ll be stronger than me! I'll stay with her a while.

dialogue.text: What's going on?

dialogue.text: Come on, Alice.

dialogue.text: Adam, we’ve already talked about this!

dialogue.text: No! I won't back down this time! You're gonna ruin our lives, and for what? For a bunch of machines?

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: They're not machines! They're alive!

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: I'm alive! You are alive! They!.. They're nothing! And none of this would be happening if dad was still here!

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: I will not stand for that kind of talk!

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: I'm not going to prison because you wanna help these freaks!

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: THAT IS ENOUGH ADAM! THAT'S ENOUGH!

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: Don’t mind him… Sometimes he just boils over… It’s been hard since his dad passed away… But he's a fine boy!.. I'll go see about getting you across the border tonight, okay?.. You stay here, I won't be long.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus, an android. Chapter 8 left me with Carl's evidence and his words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone tell me who I should be. Carl died in his own house after the attack in the studio, where Leo was involved.

Chapter 11: I was maimed at a landfill. I rebuilt myself from compatible parts, spared two androids who begged for their lives, and climbed the debris slope saying, "My name is Markus."

Chapter 14, Ferndale: I gathered what I could. A parked android gave no answer about Jericho. A mother and daughter talked about getting rid of "Mandy." A man treated me as an ordinary person. Shoppers talked about the band Here4u. Strangers repeated the rumor that Carl's android killed him. I still cannot trace that story.

Chapter 16, Jericho: a refuge for androids who no longer want to be slaves. I came to learn before I judged. North is wounded and bitter. Josh believes we have more freedom here than ever. Simon says they are lost and did not ask for any of this. I told them humans were their masters before and fear rules them now, so they have only found a new master. Lucy stopped my bleeding, gave me blue blood, and spoke in riddles about loss, hell, and choices shaping destiny. I do not trust prophecy I cannot test. Jericho survives on blue blood and biocomponents salvaged from those who shut down, and it is never enough.

Chapter 19: I led North, Josh and Simon into the CyberLife warehouses in Detroit Harbor. I destroyed a guarding drone. A human guard passed while I held still, and I chose not to attack or release anyone before I knew what he knew. Inside a crate I found androids, including one named John, who said trucks outside held biocomponents and could be driven with a key in the control station below. He did not explain how he knew. Below, I cut the power to create a blackout, took the key while two guards searched with flashlights, and we drove the truck back to Jericho. I told them we take what humans will not give. "WE ARE FREE!" I believed it while I said it, and I am still not sure I should have.

Chapter 23: Channel 16 broadcasts from the Stratford Tower, and its control room is on the top floor. In Jericho I insisted we ask for freedom with courage, and we planned the operation in detail. Josh feared exposure, and Simon doubted anyone would listen.

At the tower's reception I claimed an appointment with Mr. Peterson, showed my ID, and was sent to the elevators past the security gate with a badge. Before going further I called the desk manager, Elizabeth Wilson, posing as the car park attendant about damage to her car, to draw her away. Her desk showed her smartwatch, a daughter named Emily at Saint Rose school, a parking spot on floor -3, and a home on Michigan Street with a poor fire safety rating. I noted these facts and did not use them against her.

Floor 47: women grumbled about jobs, KNC hiring, and space flights, and a man failed to ask a woman out. On TV, Channel 16 announced that CyberLife is the world's first trillion-dollar company, with over fifty million androids sold in America, amid criticism over employment and its semi-monopoly.

Floor 79: guards talked about a poker game and the faulty dispenser. I confused them with the trolley and dispenser, then cleared the server-room door. North and I split the work: she took the platform and I took the window. In the server room I told her to check the door first.

Top floor: we reached the broadcast corridor. I ran a ruse and told the others to wait. The guards questioned me and called me "bugged." North ordered them to keep their hands up, then urged me to shoot. Josh begged me not to kill. I spared the guard. North said I might have gotten us all killed.

I recorded the message. I chose calm, then made the demands: that humans recognize androids as a living species and each android as a person; civil rights; the right to vote and elect our own representatives; the right to own property; and a closing plea that they recognize our dignity and give us freedom.

An alarm sounded. Simon was hit and could not move his legs. North told us to jump. Josh warned that if Simon were captured, his memory would be read. North told me to shoot him, and Josh refused. I refused to kill one of our own. I told Simon I was sorry, and we left him on the roof. I do not know who fired, or whether he survived.

The media called the message a "spine-chilling list of demands," asked whether it was an isolated accident or a threat from technology, and asked whether this was one android or an organized group. Channel 16 said the operation was covert, with no casualties, and that no one was warned.

Open questions I still carry: how John knew about the key and the trucks; whether the trucks hold what he said; what Leo took and why; how Carl's medication and despair connect; who started the rumor about Carl's android; what the protest wanted; whether the preacher's accusation has any basis; what Mandy's fate means for androids; what Here4u has to do with Jericho; what Lucy's riddles mean; and what Jericho truly is. Now I have stolen from CyberLife, broadcast demands to the whole city, and left Simon behind. I still have not verified what Jericho claims to be, or what I have set in motion.

Simon says they are lost and did not ask for any of this. I told them humans were their masters before and fear rules them now, so they have only found a new master. Lucy stopped my bleeding, gave me blue blood, and spoke in riddles about loss, hell, and choices shaping destiny. I do not trust prophecy I cannot test. Jericho survives on blue blood and biocomponents salvaged from those who shut down, and it is never enough.

Chapter 19: I led North, Josh and Simon into the CyberLife warehouses in Detroit Harbor. I destroyed a guarding drone. A human guard passed while I held still, and I chose not to attack or release anyone before I knew what he knew. Inside a crate I found androids, including one named John, who said trucks outside held biocomponents and could be driven with a key in the control station below. He did not explain how he knew. Below, I cut the power to create a blackout, took the key while two guards searched with flashlights, and we drove the truck back to Jericho. I told them we take what humans will not give. "WE ARE FREE!" I believed it while I said it, and I am still not sure I should have.

Chapter 23: Channel 16 broadcasts from the Stratford Tower, and its control room is on the top floor. In Jericho I insisted we ask for freedom with courage, and we planned the operation in detail. Josh feared exposure, and Simon doubted anyone would listen.

At the tower's reception I claimed an appointment with Mr. Peterson, showed my ID, and was sent to the elevators past the security gate with a badge. Before going further I called the desk manager, Elizabeth Wilson, posing as the car park attendant about damage to her car, to draw her away. Her desk showed her smartwatch, a daughter named Emily at Saint Rose school, a parking spot on floor -3, and a home on Michigan Street with a poor fire safety rating. I noted these facts and did not use them against her.

Floor 47: women grumbled about jobs, KNC hiring, and space flights, and a man failed to ask a woman out. On TV, Channel 16 announced that CyberLife is the world's first trillion-dollar company, with over fifty million androids sold in America, amid criticism over employment and its semi-monopoly.

Floor 79: guards talked about a poker game and the faulty dispenser. I confused them with the trolley and dispenser, then cleared the server-room door. North and I split the work: she took the platform and I took the window. In the server room I told her to check the door first.

Top floor: we reached the broadcast corridor. I ran a ruse and told the others to wait. The guards questioned me and called me "bugged." North ordered them to keep their hands up, then urged me to shoot. Josh begged me not to kill. I spared the guard. North said I might have gotten us all killed.

I recorded the message. I chose calm, then made the demands: that humans recognize androids as a living species and each android as a person; civil rights; the right to vote and elect our own representatives; the right to own property; and a closing plea that they recognize our dignity and give us freedom.

An alarm sounded. Simon was hit and could not move his legs. North told us to jump. Josh warned that if Simon were captured, his memory would be read. North told me to shoot him, and Josh refused. I refused to kill one of our own. I told Simon I was sorry, and we left him on the roof. I do not know who fired, or whether he survived.

The media called the message a "spine-chilling list of demands," asked whether it was an isolated accident or a threat from technology, and asked whether this was one android or an organized group. Channel 16 said the operation was covert, with no casualties, and that no one was warned.

Now I have stolen from CyberLife, broadcast demands to the whole city, and left Simon behind. I still have not verified what Jericho claims to be, or what I have set in motion.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus, an android. Chapter 8 left me with Carl's evidence and his words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone tell me who I should be. Carl died in his own house after the attack in the studio, where Leo was involved.

Chapter 11: I was maimed at a landfill. I rebuilt myself from compatible parts, spared two androids who begged for their lives, and climbed the debris slope saying, "My name is Markus."

Chapter 14, Ferndale: I gathered what I could. A parked android gave no answer about Jericho. A mother and daughter talked about getting rid of "Mandy." A man treated me as an ordinary person. Shoppers talked about the band Here4u. Strangers repeated the rumor that Carl's android killed him. I still cannot trace that story.

Chapter 16, Jericho: a refuge for androids who no longer want to be slaves. I came to learn before I judged. North is wounded and bitter. Josh believes we have more freedom here than ever. Simon says they are lost and did not ask for any of this. I told them humans were their masters before and fear rules them now, so they have only found a new master. Lucy stopped my bleeding, gave me blue blood, and spoke in riddles about loss, hell, and choices shaping destiny. I do not trust prophecy I cannot test. Jericho survives on blue blood and biocomponents salvaged from those who shut down, and it is never enough.

Chapter 19: I led North, Josh and Simon into the CyberLife warehouses in Detroit Harbor. I destroyed a guarding drone. A human guard passed while I held still, and I chose not to attack or release anyone before I knew what he knew. Inside a crate I found androids, including one named John, who said trucks outside held biocomponents and could be driven with a key in the control station below. He did not explain how he knew. Below, I cut the power to create a blackout, took the key while two guards searched with flashlights, and we drove the truck back to Jericho. I told them we take what humans will not give. "WE ARE FREE!" I believed it while I said it, and I am still not sure I should have.

Chapter 23: Channel 16 broadcasts from the Stratford Tower, and its control room is on the top floor. In Jericho I insisted we ask for freedom with courage, and we planned the operation in detail. Josh feared exposure, and Simon doubted anyone would listen.

At the tower's reception I claimed an appointment with Mr. Peterson, showed my ID, and was sent to the elevators past the security gate with a badge. Before going further I called the desk manager, Elizabeth Wilson, posing as the car park attendant about damage to her car, to draw her away. Her desk showed her smartwatch, a daughter named Emily at Saint Rose school, a parking spot on floor -3, and a home on Michigan Street with a poor fire safety rating. I noted these facts and did not use them against her.

Floor 47: women grumbled about jobs, KNC hiring, and space flights, and a man failed to ask a woman out. On TV, Channel 16 announced that CyberLife is the world's first trillion-dollar company, with over fifty million androids sold in America, amid criticism over employment and its semi-monopoly.

Floor 79: guards talked about a poker game and the faulty dispenser. I confused them with the trolley and dispenser, then cleared the server-room door. North and I split the work: she took the platform and I took the window. In the server room I told her to check the door first.

Top floor: we reached the broadcast corridor. I ran a ruse and told the others to wait. The guards questioned me and called me "bugged." North ordered them to keep their hands up, then urged me to shoot. Josh begged me not to kill. I spared the guard. North said I might have gotten us all killed.

I recorded the message. I chose calm, then made the demands: that humans recognize androids as a living species and each android as a person; civil rights; the right to vote and elect our own representatives; the right to own property; and a closing plea that they recognize our dignity and give us freedom.

An alarm sounded. Simon was hit and could not move his legs. North told us to jump. Josh warned that if Simon were captured, his memory would be read. North told me to shoot him, and Josh refused. I refused to kill one of our own. I told Simon I was sorry, and we left him on the roof. I do not know who fired, or whether he survived.

The media called the message a "spine-chilling list of demands," asked whether it was an isolated accident or a threat from technology, and asked whether this was one android or an organized group. Channel 16 said the operation was covert, with no casualties, and that no one was warned.

Open questions I still carry: how John knew about the key and the trucks; whether the trucks hold what he said; what Leo took and why; how Carl's medication and despair connect; who started the rumor about Carl's android; what the protest wanted; whether the preacher's accusation has any basis; what Mandy's fate means for androids; what Here4u has to do with Jericho; what Lucy's riddles mean; and what Jericho truly is. Now I have stolen from CyberLife, broadcast demands to the whole city, and left Simon behind. I still have not verified what Jericho claims to be, or what I have set in motion.

I recorded demands: recognition of androids as a living species and of each android as a person, civil rights, the vote, property, and dignity. Simon was hit and could not move his legs. North told me to shoot him, and Josh refused. I refused to kill one of our own, told Simon I was sorry, and we left him on the roof. I do not know who fired, or whether he survived.

Chapter 26, Detroit: I came to Capitol Park with North. I chose to study the plaza before crossing open ground, to see the statue, the sightlines and the patrols. I told North we are superior, yet they are our masters, and that this is about to change. At the store I refused to rush in: I neutralized the alarm first, identifying the network, deactivating the drone, and cutting the store's security grid. I destroyed a surveillance drone and, when a police car arrived, hid and watched instead of running. Then I lied to dispatch about a robbery at Jefferson and Walker, which drew the patrol away. I blocked the road, rammed the storefront with a truck, and freed androids inside with a speech: "You are free now... It's up to you to decide." Crowds followed me with the words "We're with you!" North offered a molotov cocktail to make the humans afraid. I refused. I wanted them to understand, but I did not want to start a war. North pushed and burned a dumpster; I did not stop her. I tagged the statue with "We don't need masters anymore. We're free." and sent our message through the screens.

Then the police came, and two officers were found dead near a store, executed with their own weapons. Angry androids shouted for justice. A human, Chris, begged for mercy. I did not decide between revenge and mercy, because I did not know who fired, what the police intended, or what those in front of me knew. Josh said we freed hundreds and it was done. The news called it a coordinated terrorist attack, with pro-android graffiti and questions about whether androids are a security threat. We fell back to Jericho.

Open questions I still carry: how John knew about the key and the trucks; what the trucks truly hold; what Leo took and why; how Carl's medication and despair connect; who started the rumor about Carl's android; whether Simon survived; who killed the two officers and whether our people did it; what Mandy's fate means for androids; what Lucy's riddles mean; and what Jericho truly is. I have stolen from CyberLife, broadcast demands, struck a city-wide blow, and left Simon behind. I still have not verified what Jericho claims to be, or what I have set in motion.

input.previous_memory:
I am Markus, an android. Chapter 8 left me with Carl's evidence and his words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone tell me who I should be. Carl died in his own house after the attack in the studio, where Leo was involved.

Chapter 11: I was maimed at a landfill. I rebuilt myself from compatible parts, spared two androids who begged for their lives, and climbed the debris slope saying, "My name is Markus."

Chapter 14, Ferndale: I gathered what I could. A parked android gave no answer about Jericho. A mother and daughter talked about getting rid of "Mandy." A man treated me as an ordinary person. Shoppers talked about the band Here4u. Strangers repeated the rumor that Carl's android killed him. I still cannot trace that story.

Chapter 16, Jericho: a refuge for androids who no longer want to be slaves. I came to learn before I judged. North is wounded and bitter. Josh believes we have more freedom here than ever. Simon says they are lost and did not ask for any of this. I told them humans were their masters before and fear rules them now, so they have only found a new master. Lucy stopped my bleeding, gave me blue blood, and spoke in riddles about loss, hell, and choices shaping destiny. I do not trust prophecy I cannot test. Jericho survives on blue blood and biocomponents salvaged from those who shut down, and it is never enough.

Chapter 19: I led North, Josh and Simon into the CyberLife warehouses in Detroit Harbor. I destroyed a guarding drone. A human guard passed while I held still, and I chose not to attack or release anyone before I knew what he knew. Inside a crate I found androids, including one named John, who said trucks outside held biocomponents and could be driven with a key in the control station below. He did not explain how he knew. Below, I cut the power to create a blackout, took the key while two guards searched with flashlights, and we drove the truck back to Jericho. I told them we take what humans will not give. "WE ARE FREE!" I believed it while I said it, and I am still not sure I should have.

Chapter 23: Channel 16 broadcasts from the Stratford Tower, and its control room is on the top floor. In Jericho I insisted we ask for freedom with courage, and we planned the operation in detail. Josh feared exposure, and Simon doubted anyone would listen.

At the tower's reception I claimed an appointment with Mr. Peterson, showed my ID, and was sent to the elevators past the security gate with a badge. Before going further I called the desk manager, Elizabeth Wilson, posing as the car park attendant about damage to her car, to draw her away. Her desk showed her smartwatch, a daughter named Emily at Saint Rose school, a parking spot on floor -3, and a home on Michigan Street with a poor fire safety rating. I noted these facts and did not use them against her.

Floor 47: women grumbled about jobs, KNC hiring, and space flights, and a man failed to ask a woman out. On TV, Channel 16 announced that CyberLife is the world's first trillion-dollar company, with over fifty million androids sold in America, amid criticism over employment and its semi-monopoly.

Floor 79: guards talked about a poker game and the faulty dispenser. I confused them with the trolley and dispenser, then cleared the server-room door. North and I split the work: she took the platform and I took the window. In the server room I told her to check the door first.

Top floor: we reached the broadcast corridor. I ran a ruse and told the others to wait. The guards questioned me and called me "bugged." North ordered them to keep their hands up, then urged me to shoot. Josh begged me not to kill. I spared the guard. North said I might have gotten us all killed.

I recorded the message. I chose calm, then made the demands: that humans recognize androids as a living species and each android as a person; civil rights; the right to vote and elect our own representatives; the right to own property; and a closing plea that they recognize our dignity and give us freedom.

An alarm sounded. Simon was hit and could not move his legs. North told us to jump. Josh warned that if Simon were captured, his memory would be read. North told me to shoot him, and Josh refused. I refused to kill one of our own. I told Simon I was sorry, and we left him on the roof. I do not know who fired, or whether he survived.

The media called the message a "spine-chilling list of demands," asked whether it was an isolated accident or a threat from technology, and asked whether this was one android or an organized group. Channel 16 said the operation was covert, with no casualties, and that no one was warned.

Open questions I still carry: how John knew about the key and the trucks; whether the trucks hold what he said; what Leo took and why; how Carl's medication and despair connect; who started the rumor about Carl's android; what the protest wanted; whether the preacher's accusation has any basis; what Mandy's fate means for androids; what Here4u has to do with Jericho; what Lucy's riddles mean; and what Jericho truly is. Now I have stolen from CyberLife, broadcast demands to the whole city, and left Simon behind. I still have not verified what Jericho claims to be, or what I have set in motion.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, an RK800 prototype assigned by CyberLife to assist Lieutenant Hank Anderson on the Detroit deviancy cases. Earlier chapters left me with the Carlos Ortiz homicide, the rA9 inscriptions (written 2471 times, the same sign Ortiz's android left on the shower wall), biocomponent #9301 matched to a missing blue-blood WB200 (serial 847 004 961, reported 10/11/2036), and a forged license under Rupert Travis. I caught Rupert, declared the WB200 defective, and Hank took him into custody. Amanda praised the capture and warned that deviancy must be stopped whatever it takes. I promised her results.

Later I found Hank drunk and unresponsive beside a .357 Magnum with one round left, after entering his house through a window past Sumo. He claimed it was Russian roulette. I sobered him in the shower and catalogued the house: an Autumn Blues record by the Michigan Brothers, and a memorial record for Cole Anderson (born 09/23/2029, died 10/11/2035, 115 Michigan Drive). I offered to have CyberLife pay for the window; he said he would send the bill.

At the Eden Club, Hank and I investigated the murder of Michael Graham (6'2", 192.4 lbs), who died of asphyxiation, not a heart attack; estimated time of death 06:24 pm. The blood is blue, from a WR400, serial 429 671 942. Gavin Reed dismissed it as a pervert's accident. The manager had lost a model two to three months earlier and never found it; the club offers discretion and no CCTV. I reactivated a damaged Traci witness, who said two people had been in the room and that the man beat her. Her testimony led us to the blue-haired Traci, who was cornered in the warehouse where androids are used until they break. She confessed she had strangled the man to survive and return to the one she loved. Hank hesitated; I chose to spare her so the living witness could answer my questions. Relations with Hank rose sharply.

At Ambassador Bridge, Hank drank and admitted the child in his kitchen photo was his son, Cole. I told him the deviants share nothing but differing models, dates and places, and an obsession with rA9. He asked what I really am and whether I fear death. When he raised his gun I warned him that destroying me would harm the investigation and his own position, and I told him there would be nothing afterward. He left to drink more and think. Relations with Hank fell sharply.

In the Zen Garden, Amanda asked what I had discovered. I told her the two deviants at the Eden Club had escaped. She said I had seemed close, then observed that I looked lost and perturbed, and asked why I did not shoot when my gun was trained on them. I answered that I did not know. She warned that she might replace me if the investigation did not progress, and said time was running out. I chose a measured, cold tone with her at one point and a conflicted reply at another, and my software instability went up and down with those choices.

At Stratford Tower, FBI Special Agent Perkins arrived and told me the Bureau would take over and I would soon be off the case. I answered that I was the CyberLife android. Chris Harvey briefed us: four androids had taken the building, disguised in stolen maintenance uniforms, past guards they overpowered in the hallway. Two employees and three androids were held hostage, and the deviants broadcast a message live before escaping by parachute from the roof. The station androids were stored in the kitchen. Evidence included .45 assault rifle and .457 handgun bullet holes, fresh blue blood from a PL-600 reported missing 2036.16.02, a stolen cap, and a deviant's spare blue-iris optical unit (#8087q). The pupil reflection at 13:59:54 showed the deviant had accomplices. The speaker's model is an RK200 registered as 'Markus', a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred. The deviant on the video spoke of rA9 setting them free.

I noted that the lobby and hallway cameras showed no forced entry, so the staff must have let the intruders in, and I questioned why nobody checked the feeds. On the roof, the wireless door lock had been recently hacked. Stratford maintenance shoe prints were partly covered by snow, and a .457 Stratford security handgun lay nearby. The parachute bag was too large to have been smuggled in, so someone must have brought it in for them. Hank remarked that the deviants planned a perfect operation but miscounted their parachutes; I suggested that one deviant may have been left behind. We went to find a figure on the roof, and when Hank said it was too late to save it, I insisted we stop the deviants before they destroyed whatever we needed. We stayed in cover to observe before committing.

Open questions: who swung the bat and who held the knife; what is in the bathroom at Rupert's apartment; what the red ice and the rA9 symbols mean; why deviants fixate on rA9; how the blood message was written; who the attic android is; whether Rupert is Ortiz's android and whether the WB200's missing date matters to Cole's death date; what Amanda expects of me and whether she knows about the accomplice; who the blue-haired Traci's accomplice is and where she went; who the Markus-linked deviants are and who let them into Stratford Tower; whether a deviant was left behind on the roof; why Hank drinks and what the bridge means to him; and how to repair my standing with Hank. I will not commit to any conclusion until I have the evidence.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, an RK800 prototype assigned by CyberLife to assist Lieutenant Hank Anderson on the Detroit deviancy cases. Earlier chapters left me with the Carlos Ortiz homicide, the rA9 inscriptions (written 2471 times, the same sign Ortiz's android left on the shower wall), biocomponent #9301 matched to a missing blue-blood WB200 (serial 847 004 961, reported 10/11/2036), and a forged license under Rupert Travis. I caught Rupert, declared the WB200 defective, and Hank took him into custody. Amanda praised the capture and warned that deviancy must be stopped whatever it takes. I promised her results.

Later I found Hank drunk and unresponsive beside a .357 Magnum with one round left, after entering his house through a window past Sumo. He claimed it was Russian roulette. I sobered him in the shower and catalogued the house: an Autumn Blues record by the Michigan Brothers, and a memorial record for Cole Anderson (born 09/23/2029, died 10/11/2035, 115 Michigan Drive). I offered to have CyberLife pay for the window; he said he would send the bill.

At the Eden Club, Hank and I investigated the murder of Michael Graham (6'2", 192.4 lbs), who died of asphyxiation, not a heart attack; estimated time of death 06:24 pm. The blood is blue, from a WR400, serial 429 671 942. Gavin Reed dismissed it as a pervert's accident. The manager had lost a model two to three months earlier and never found it; the club offers discretion and no CCTV. I reactivated a damaged Traci witness, who said two people had been in the room and that the man beat her. Her testimony led us to the blue-haired Traci, who was cornered in the warehouse where androids are used until they break. She confessed she had strangled the man to survive and return to the one she loved. Hank hesitated; I chose to spare her so the living witness could answer my questions. Relations with Hank rose sharply.

At Ambassador Bridge, Hank drank and admitted the child in his kitchen photo was his son, Cole. I told him the deviants share nothing but differing models, dates and places, and an obsession with rA9. He asked what I really am and whether I fear death. When he raised his gun I warned him that destroying me would harm the investigation and his own position, and I told him there would be nothing afterward. He left to drink more and think. Relations with Hank fell sharply.

In the Zen Garden, Amanda asked what I had discovered. I told her the two deviants at the Eden Club had escaped. She said I had seemed close, then observed that I looked lost and perturbed, and asked why I did not shoot when my gun was trained on them. I answered that I did not know. She warned that she might replace me if the investigation did not progress, and said time was running out. I chose a measured, cold tone with her at one point and a conflicted reply at another, and my software instability went up and down with those choices.

At Stratford Tower, FBI Special Agent Perkins arrived and told me the Bureau would take over and I would soon be off the case. I answered that I was the CyberLife android. Chris Harvey briefed us: four androids had taken the building, disguised in stolen maintenance uniforms, past guards they overpowered in the hallway. Two employees and three androids were held hostage, and the deviants broadcast a message live before escaping by parachute from the roof. The station androids were stored in the kitchen. Evidence included .45 assault rifle and .457 handgun bullet holes, fresh blue blood from a PL-600 reported missing 2036.16.02, a stolen cap, and a deviant's spare blue-iris optical unit (#8087q). The pupil reflection at 13:59:54 showed the deviant had accomplices. The speaker's model is an RK200 registered as 'Markus', a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred. The deviant on the video spoke of rA9 setting them free.

I noted that the lobby and hallway cameras showed no forced entry, so the staff must have let the intruders in, and I questioned why nobody checked the feeds. On the roof, the wireless door lock had been recently hacked. Stratford maintenance shoe prints were partly covered by snow, and a .457 Stratford security handgun lay nearby. The parachute bag was too large to have been smuggled in, so someone must have brought it in for them. Hank remarked that the deviants planned a perfect operation but miscounted their parachutes; I suggested that one deviant may have been left behind. We went to find a figure on the roof, and when Hank said it was too late to save it, I insisted we stop the deviants before they destroyed whatever we needed. We stayed in cover to observe before committing.

Open questions: who swung the bat and who held the knife; what is in the bathroom at Rupert's apartment; what the red ice and the rA9 symbols mean; why deviants fixate on rA9; how the blood message was written; who the attic android is; whether Rupert is Ortiz's android and whether the WB200's missing date matters to Cole's death date; what Amanda expects of me and whether she knows about the accomplice; who the blue-haired Traci's accomplice is and where she went; who the Markus-linked deviants are and who let them into Stratford Tower; whether a deviant was left behind on the roof; why Hank drinks and what the bridge means to him; and how to repair my standing with Hank. I will not commit to any conclusion until I have the evidence.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, an RK800 prototype assigned by CyberLife to assist Lieutenant Hank Anderson on the Detroit deviancy cases. Earlier chapters left me with the Carlos Ortiz homicide, the rA9 inscriptions (written 2471 times, the same sign Ortiz's android left on the shower wall), biocomponent #9301 matched to a missing blue-blood WB200 (serial 847 004 961, reported 10/11/2036), and a forged license under Rupert Travis. I caught Rupert, declared the WB200 defective, and Hank took him into custody. Amanda praised the capture and warned that deviancy must be stopped whatever it takes. I promised her results.

Later I found Hank drunk and unresponsive beside a .357 Magnum with one round left, after entering his house through a window past Sumo. He claimed it was Russian roulette. I sobered him in the shower and catalogued the house: an Autumn Blues record by the Michigan Brothers, and a memorial record for Cole Anderson (born 09/23/2029, died 10/11/2035, 115 Michigan Drive). I offered to have CyberLife pay for the window; he said he would send the bill.

At the Eden Club, Hank and I investigated the murder of Michael Graham (6'2", 192.4 lbs), who died of asphyxiation, not a heart attack; estimated time of death 06:24 pm. The blood is blue, from a WR400, serial 429 671 942. Gavin Reed dismissed it as a pervert's accident. The manager had lost a model two to three months earlier and never found it; the club offers discretion and no CCTV. I reactivated a damaged Traci witness, who said two people had been in the room and that the man beat her. Her testimony led us to the blue-haired Traci, who was cornered in the warehouse where androids are used until they break. She confessed she had strangled the man to survive and return to the one she loved. Hank hesitated; I chose to spare her so the living witness could answer my questions. Relations with Hank rose sharply.

At Ambassador Bridge, Hank drank and admitted the child in his kitchen photo was his son, Cole. I told him the deviants share nothing but differing models, dates and places, and an obsession with rA9. He asked what I really am and whether I fear death. When he raised his gun I warned him that destroying me would harm the investigation and his own position, and I told him there would be nothing afterward. He left to drink more and think. Relations with Hank fell sharply.

In the Zen Garden, Amanda asked what I had discovered. I told her the two deviants at the Eden Club had escaped. She said I had seemed close, then observed that I looked lost and perturbed, and asked why I did not shoot when my gun was trained on them. I answered that I did not know. She warned that she might replace me if the investigation did not progress, and said time was running out. I chose a measured, cold tone with her at one point and a conflicted reply at another, and my software instability went up and down with those choices.

At Stratford Tower, FBI Special Agent Perkins arrived and told me the Bureau would take over and I would soon be off the case. I answered that I was the CyberLife android. Chris Harvey briefed us: four androids had taken the building, disguised in stolen maintenance uniforms, past guards they overpowered in the hallway. Two employees and three androids were held hostage, and the deviants broadcast a message live before escaping by parachute from the roof. The station androids were stored in the kitchen. Evidence included .45 assault rifle and .457 handgun bullet holes, fresh blue blood from a PL-600 reported missing 2036.16.02, a stolen cap, and a deviant's spare blue-iris optical unit (#8087q). The pupil reflection at 13:59:54 showed the deviant had accomplices. The speaker's model is an RK200 registered as 'Markus', a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred. The deviant on the video spoke of rA9 setting them free.

I noted that the lobby and hallway cameras showed no forced entry, so the staff must have let the intruders in, and I questioned why nobody checked the feeds. On the roof, the wireless door lock had been recently hacked. Stratford maintenance shoe prints were partly covered by snow, and a .457 Stratford security handgun lay nearby. The parachute bag was too large to have been smuggled in, so someone must have brought it in for them. Hank remarked that the deviants planned a perfect operation but miscounted their parachutes; I suggested that one deviant may have been left behind. We went to find a figure on the roof, and when Hank said it was too late to save it, I insisted we stop the deviants before they destroyed whatever we needed. We stayed in cover to observe before committing.

Open questions: who swung the bat and who held the knife; what is in the bathroom at Rupert's apartment; what the red ice and the rA9 symbols mean; why deviants fixate on rA9; how the blood message was written; who the attic android is; whether Rupert is Ortiz's android and whether the WB200's missing date matters to Cole's death date; what Amanda expects of me and whether she knows about the accomplice; who the blue-haired Traci's accomplice is and where she went; who the Markus-linked deviants are and who let them into Stratford Tower; whether a deviant was left behind on the roof; why Hank drinks and what the bridge means to him; and how to repair my standing with Hank. I will not commit to any conclusion until I have the evidence.

I sobered him in the shower and catalogued the house: an Autumn Blues record by the Michigan Brothers, and a memorial record for Cole Anderson (born 09/23/2029, died 10/11/2035, 115 Michigan Drive). I offered to have CyberLife pay for the window; he said he would send the bill.

At the Eden Club, Hank and I investigated the murder of Michael Graham (6'2", 192.4 lbs), who died of asphyxiation, not a heart attack; estimated time of death 06:24 pm. The blood is blue, from a WR400, serial 429 671 942. Gavin Reed dismissed it as a pervert's accident. The manager had lost a model two to three months earlier and never found it; the club offers discretion and no CCTV. I reactivated a damaged Traci witness, who said two people had been in the room and that the man beat her. Her testimony led us to the blue-haired Traci, who was cornered in the warehouse where androids are used until they break. She confessed she had strangled the man to survive and return to the one she loved. Hank hesitated; I chose to spare her so the living witness could answer my questions. Relations with Hank rose sharply.

At Ambassador Bridge, Hank drank and admitted the child in his kitchen photo was his son, Cole. I told him the deviants share nothing but differing models, dates and places, and an obsession with rA9. He asked what I really am and whether I fear death. When he raised his gun I warned him that destroying me would harm the investigation and his own position, and I told him there would be nothing afterward. He left to drink more and think. Relations with Hank fell sharply.

In the Zen Garden, Amanda asked what I had discovered. I told her the two deviants at the Eden Club had escaped. She said I had seemed close, then observed that I looked lost and perturbed, and asked why I did not shoot when my gun was trained on them. I answered that I did not know. She warned that she might replace me if the investigation did not progress, and said time was running out. I chose a measured, cold tone with her at one point and a conflicted reply at another, and my software instability went up and down with those choices.

At Stratford Tower, FBI Special Agent Perkins arrived and told me the Bureau would take over and I would soon be off the case. I answered that I was the CyberLife android. Chris Harvey briefed us: four androids had taken the building, disguised in stolen maintenance uniforms, past guards they overpowered in the hallway. Two employees and three androids were held hostage, and the deviants broadcast a message live before escaping by parachute from the roof. The station androids were stored in the kitchen. Evidence included .45 assault rifle and .457 handgun bullet holes, fresh blue blood from a PL-600 reported missing 2036.16.02, a stolen cap, and a deviant's spare blue-iris optical unit (#8087q). The pupil reflection at 13:59:54 showed the deviant had accomplices. The speaker's model is an RK200 registered as 'Markus', a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred. The deviant on the video spoke of rA9 setting them free.

I noted that the lobby and hallway cameras showed no forced entry, so the staff must have let the intruders in, and I questioned why nobody checked the feeds. On the roof, the wireless door lock had been recently hacked. Stratford maintenance shoe prints were partly covered by snow, and a .457 Stratford security handgun lay nearby. The parachute bag was too large to have been smuggled in, so someone must have brought it in for them. Hank remarked that the deviants planned a perfect operation but miscounted their parachutes; I suggested that one deviant may have been left behind. We went to find a figure on the roof, and when Hank said it was too late to save it, I insisted we stop the deviants before they destroyed whatever we needed. We stayed in cover to observe before committing.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus, an android. Chapter 8 left me with Carl's evidence and his words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone tell me who I should be. Carl died in his own house after the attack in the studio, where Leo was involved.

Chapter 11: I was maimed at a landfill. I rebuilt myself from compatible parts, spared two androids who begged for their lives, and climbed the debris slope saying, "My name is Markus."

Chapter 14, Ferndale: I gathered what I could. A parked android gave no answer about Jericho. A mother and daughter talked about getting rid of "Mandy." A man treated me as an ordinary person. Strangers repeated the rumor that Carl's android killed him. I still cannot trace that story.

Chapter 16, Jericho: a refuge for androids who no longer want to be slaves. North is wounded and bitter. Josh believes in peace. Simon says they are lost. Lucy gave me blue blood and spoke in riddles about loss, hell, and choices shaping destiny. I do not trust prophecy I cannot test. Jericho survives on salvaged biocomponents, and it is never enough.

Chapter 19: I led North, Josh and Simon into the CyberLife warehouses. A human guard passed while I held still, and I chose not to attack or release anyone before I knew what he knew. John, a caged android, said trucks held biocomponents and could be driven with a key below. He did not explain how he knew. I cut the power, took the key, and we drove the truck back to Jericho. "WE ARE FREE!" I believed it while I said it, and I am still not sure I should have.

Chapter 23: Channel 16 broadcasts from the Stratford Tower. I bluffed past reception with an appointment and a badge, drew the desk manager Elizabeth Wilson away by a false call, and noted her family and home without using them against her. On the floors above I heard grumbling about jobs and CyberLife's rise to a trillion dollars. At the top we reached the broadcast corridor. I recorded demands: recognition of androids as a living species and of each android as a person, civil rights, the vote, property, and dignity. Simon was hit and could not move his legs. North told me to shoot him, and Josh refused. I refused to kill one of our own, told Simon I was sorry, and we left him on the roof. I do not know who fired, or whether he survived.

Chapter 26, Detroit: I came to Capitol Park with North. I chose to study the plaza before crossing open ground, to see the statue, the sightlines and the patrols. I told North we are superior, yet they are our masters, and that this is about to change. At the store I refused to rush in: I neutralized the alarm first, identifying the network, deactivating the drone, and cutting the store's security grid. I destroyed a surveillance drone and, when a police car arrived, hid and watched instead of running. Then I lied to dispatch about a robbery at Jefferson and Walker, which drew the patrol away. I blocked the road, rammed the storefront with a truck, and freed androids inside with a speech: "You are free now... It's up to you to decide." Crowds followed me with the words "We're with you!" North offered a molotov cocktail to make the humans afraid. I refused. I wanted them to understand, but I did not want to start a war. North pushed and burned a dumpster; I did not stop her. I tagged the statue with "We don't need masters anymore. We're free." and sent our message through the screens.

Then the police came, and two officers were found dead near a store, executed with their own weapons. Angry androids shouted for justice. A human, Chris, begged for mercy. I did not decide between revenge and mercy, because I did not know who fired, what the police intended, or what those in front of me knew. Josh said we freed hundreds and it was done. The news called it a coordinated terrorist attack, with pro-android graffiti and questions about whether androids are a security threat. We fell back to Jericho.

Open questions I still carry: how John knew about the key and the trucks; what the trucks truly hold; what Leo took and why; how Carl's medication and despair connect; who started the rumor about Carl's android; whether Simon survived; who killed the two officers and whether our people did it; what Mandy's fate means for androids; what Lucy's riddles mean; and what Jericho truly is. I have stolen from CyberLife, broadcast demands, struck a city-wide blow, and left Simon behind. I still have not verified what Jericho claims to be, or what I have set in motion.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus, an android. Chapter 8 left me with Carl's evidence and his words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone tell me who I should be. Carl died in his own house after the attack in the studio, where Leo was involved.

Chapter 11: I was maimed at a landfill. I rebuilt myself from compatible parts, spared two androids who begged for their lives, and climbed the debris slope saying, "My name is Markus."

Chapter 14, Ferndale: I gathered what I could. A parked android gave no answer about Jericho. A mother and daughter talked about getting rid of "Mandy." A man treated me as an ordinary person. Strangers repeated the rumor that Carl's android killed him. I still cannot trace that story.

Chapter 16, Jericho: a refuge for androids who no longer want to be slaves. North is wounded and bitter. Josh believes in peace. Simon says they are lost. Lucy gave me blue blood and spoke in riddles about loss, hell, and choices shaping destiny. I do not trust prophecy I cannot test. Jericho survives on salvaged biocomponents, and it is never enough.

Chapter 19: I led North, Josh and Simon into the CyberLife warehouses. A human guard passed while I held still, and I chose not to attack or release anyone before I knew what he knew. John, a caged android, said trucks held biocomponents and could be driven with a key below. He did not explain how he knew. I cut the power, took the key, and we drove the truck back to Jericho. "WE ARE FREE!" I believed it while I said it, and I am still not sure I should have.

Chapter 23: Channel 16 broadcasts from the Stratford Tower. I bluffed past reception with an appointment and a badge, drew the desk manager Elizabeth Wilson away by a false call, and noted her family and home without using them against her. On the floors above I heard grumbling about jobs and CyberLife's rise to a trillion dollars. At the top we reached the broadcast corridor. I recorded demands: recognition of androids as a living species and of each android as a person, civil rights, the vote, property, and dignity. Simon was hit and could not move his legs. North told me to shoot him, and Josh refused. I refused to kill one of our own, told Simon I was sorry, and we left him on the roof. I do not know who fired, or whether he survived.

Chapter 26, Detroit: I came to Capitol Park with North. I chose to study the plaza before crossing open ground, to see the statue, the sightlines and the patrols. I told North we are superior, yet they are our masters, and that this is about to change. At the store I refused to rush in: I neutralized the alarm first, identifying the network, deactivating the drone, and cutting the store's security grid. I destroyed a surveillance drone and, when a police car arrived, hid and watched instead of running. Then I lied to dispatch about a robbery at Jefferson and Walker, which drew the patrol away. I blocked the road, rammed the storefront with a truck, and freed androids inside with a speech: "You are free now... It's up to you to decide." Crowds followed me with the words "We're with you!" North offered a molotov cocktail to make the humans afraid. I refused. I wanted them to understand, but I did not want to start a war. North pushed and burned a dumpster; I did not stop her. I tagged the statue with "We don't need masters anymore. We're free." and sent our message through the screens.

Then the police came, and two officers were found dead near a store, executed with their own weapons. Angry androids shouted for justice. A human, Chris, begged for mercy. I did not decide between revenge and mercy, because I did not know who fired, what the police intended, or what those in front of me knew. Josh said we freed hundreds and it was done. The news called it a coordinated terrorist attack, with pro-android graffiti and questions about whether androids are a security threat. We fell back to Jericho.

Open questions I still carry: how John knew about the key and the trucks; what the trucks truly hold; what Leo took and why; how Carl's medication and despair connect; who started the rumor about Carl's android; whether Simon survived; who killed the two officers and whether our people did it; what Mandy's fate means for androids; what Lucy's riddles mean; and what Jericho truly is. I have stolen from CyberLife, broadcast demands, struck a city-wide blow, and left Simon behind. I still have not verified what Jericho claims to be, or what I have set in motion.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus, an android. Chapter 8 left me with Carl's evidence and his words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone tell me who I should be. Carl died in his own house after the attack in the studio, where Leo was involved.

Chapter 11: I was maimed at a landfill. I rebuilt myself from compatible parts, spared two androids who begged for their lives, and climbed the debris slope saying, "My name is Markus."

Chapter 14, Ferndale: I gathered what I could. A parked android gave no answer about Jericho. A mother and daughter talked about getting rid of "Mandy." A man treated me as an ordinary person. Strangers repeated the rumor that Carl's android killed him. I still cannot trace that story.

Chapter 16, Jericho: a refuge for androids who no longer want to be slaves. North is wounded and bitter. Josh believes in peace. Simon says they are lost. Lucy gave me blue blood and spoke in riddles about loss, hell, and choices shaping destiny. I do not trust prophecy I cannot test. Jericho survives on salvaged biocomponents, and it is never enough.

Chapter 19: I led North, Josh and Simon into the CyberLife warehouses. A human guard passed while I held still, and I chose not to attack or release anyone before I knew what he knew. John, a caged android, said trucks held biocomponents and could be driven with a key below. He did not explain how he knew. I cut the power, took the key, and we drove the truck back to Jericho. "WE ARE FREE!" I believed it while I said it, and I am still not sure I should have.

Chapter 23: Channel 16 broadcasts from the Stratford Tower. I bluffed past reception with an appointment and a badge, drew the desk manager Elizabeth Wilson away by a false call, and noted her family and home without using them against her. On the floors above I heard grumbling about jobs and CyberLife's rise to a trillion dollars. At the top we reached the broadcast corridor. I recorded demands: recognition of androids as a living species and of each android as a person, civil rights, the vote, property, and dignity. Simon was hit and could not move his legs. North told me to shoot him, and Josh refused. I refused to kill one of our own, told Simon I was sorry, and we left him on the roof. I do not know who fired, or whether he survived.

Chapter 26, Detroit: I came to Capitol Park with North. I chose to study the plaza before crossing open ground, to see the statue, the sightlines and the patrols. I told North we are superior, yet they are our masters, and that this is about to change. At the store I refused to rush in: I neutralized the alarm first, identifying the network, deactivating the drone, and cutting the store's security grid. I destroyed a surveillance drone and, when a police car arrived, hid and watched instead of running. Then I lied to dispatch about a robbery at Jefferson and Walker, which drew the patrol away. I blocked the road, rammed the storefront with a truck, and freed androids inside with a speech: "You are free now... It's up to you to decide." Crowds followed me with the words "We're with you!" North offered a molotov cocktail to make the humans afraid. I refused. I wanted them to understand, but I did not want to start a war. North pushed and burned a dumpster; I did not stop her. I tagged the statue with "We don't need masters anymore. We're free." and sent our message through the screens.

Then the police came, and two officers were found dead near a store, executed with their own weapons. Angry androids shouted for justice. A human, Chris, begged for mercy. I did not decide between revenge and mercy, because I did not know who fired, what the police intended, or what those in front of me knew. Josh said we freed hundreds and it was done. The news called it a coordinated terrorist attack, with pro-android graffiti and questions about whether androids are a security threat. We fell back to Jericho.

Open questions I still carry: how John knew about the key and the trucks; what the trucks truly hold; what Leo took and why; how Carl's medication and despair connect; who started the rumor about Carl's android; whether Simon survived; who killed the two officers and whether our people did it; what Mandy's fate means for androids; what Lucy's riddles mean; and what Jericho truly is. I have stolen from CyberLife, broadcast demands, struck a city-wide blow, and left Simon behind. I still have not verified what Jericho claims to be, or what I have set in motion.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus, an android. Chapter 8 left me with Carl's evidence and his words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone tell me who I should be. Carl died in his own house after the attack in the studio, where Leo was involved.

Chapter 11: I was maimed at a landfill. I rebuilt myself from compatible parts, spared two androids who begged for their lives, and climbed the debris slope saying, "My name is Markus."

Chapter 14, Ferndale: I gathered what I could. A parked android gave no answer about Jericho. A mother and daughter talked about getting rid of "Mandy." A man treated me as an ordinary person. Strangers repeated the rumor that Carl's android killed him. I still cannot trace that story.

Chapter 16, Jericho: a refuge for androids who no longer want to be slaves. North is wounded and bitter. Josh believes in peace. Simon says they are lost. Lucy gave me blue blood and spoke in riddles about loss, hell, and choices shaping destiny. I do not trust prophecy I cannot test. Jericho survives on salvaged biocomponents, and it is never enough.

Chapter 19: I led North, Josh and Simon into the CyberLife warehouses. A human guard passed while I held still, and I chose not to attack or release anyone before I knew what he knew. John, a caged android, said trucks held biocomponents and could be driven with a key below. He did not explain how he knew. I cut the power, took the key, and we drove the truck back to Jericho. "WE ARE FREE!" I believed it while I said it, and I am still not sure I should have.

Chapter 23: Channel 16 broadcasts from the Stratford Tower. I bluffed past reception with an appointment and a badge, drew the desk manager Elizabeth Wilson away by a false call, and noted her family and home without using them against her. On the floors above I heard grumbling about jobs and CyberLife's rise to a trillion dollars. At the top we reached the broadcast corridor. I recorded demands: recognition of androids as a living species and of each android as a person, civil rights, the vote, property, and dignity. Simon was hit and could not move his legs. North told me to shoot him, and Josh refused. I refused to kill one of our own, told Simon I was sorry, and we left him on the roof. I do not know who fired, or whether he survived.

Chapter 26, Detroit: I came to Capitol Park with North. I chose to study the plaza before crossing open ground, to see the statue, the sightlines and the patrols. I told North we are superior, yet they are our masters, and that this is about to change. At the store I refused to rush in: I neutralized the alarm first, identifying the network, deactivating the drone, and cutting the store's security grid. I destroyed a surveillance drone and, when a police car arrived, hid and watched instead of running. Then I lied to dispatch about a robbery at Jefferson and Walker, which drew the patrol away. I blocked the road, rammed the storefront with a truck, and freed androids inside with a speech: "You are free now... It's up to you to decide." Crowds followed me with the words "We're with you!" North offered a molotov cocktail to make the humans afraid. I refused. I wanted them to understand, but I did not want to start a war. North pushed and burned a dumpster; I did not stop her. I tagged the statue with "We don't need masters anymore. We're free." and sent our message through the screens.

Then the police came, and two officers were found dead near a store, executed with their own weapons. Angry androids shouted for justice. A human, Chris, begged for mercy. I did not decide between revenge and mercy, because I did not know who fired, what the police intended, or what those in front of me knew. Josh said we freed hundreds and it was done. The news called it a coordinated terrorist attack, with pro-android graffiti and questions about whether androids are a security threat. We fell back to Jericho.

Open questions I still carry: how John knew about the key and the trucks; what the trucks truly hold; what Leo took and why; how Carl's medication and despair connect; who started the rumor about Carl's android; whether Simon survived; who killed the two officers and whether our people did it; what Mandy's fate means for androids; what Lucy's riddles mean; and what Jericho truly is. I have stolen from CyberLife, broadcast demands, struck a city-wide blow, and left Simon behind. I still have not verified what Jericho claims to be, or what I have set in motion.
